During the Later Wei dynasty, there was Lu Jingyu, courtesy name Zhongru, a descendant of Jie Min. Initially serving as a *Guoziboshi* (State Academy Doctor), he was a believer in the Śākya teachings and had annotated the *Zhouyi* and the *Lunyu*.
His elder cousin, Shenli, led a local rebellion and coerced him into joining forces to respond to the Western Wei.

While imprisoned in the Jinyang jail, he recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* with single-minded devotion, whereupon his shackles and chains fell away of their own accord. When Qi Shiwu served as Chancellor...
A Special Case of Pardon (from the *Baoying ji*).

Zhao Wenruo of the Sui dynasty died of illness at the beginning of the Kaihuang era. After seven days had passed, his family was about to prepare him for burial when he suddenly shrank [in size] by one... [inch].
His feet then stopped, and upon regaining consciousness, he said: "A man came to pursue me, and I immediately followed him. We entered a palace city where I saw a king.
The king asked, 'What meritorious deeds did you perform while alive? I replied, 'I only upheld the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. The king said, 'This is the most supreme.
Although your allotted lifespan has ended, because of your upholding of this sūtra, it shall be extended for you. He further said, 'Among all sins, killing..."
The suffering is extremely severe. How can you remain satiated with pigs and sheep? He immediately dispatched a messenger with the decree.
Upon reaching the place of suffering, one travels north for two or three *li* until arriving at the base of a high wall. There is a hole there, just large enough for a person to fit through.

Emerging from this hole, one ascends a high mound; looking out in all directions, the expanse is vast and wide. One sees a city that is exceedingly high and steep, its smoke and fire reaching to the heavens, black—
His vital energy overflowed from his body, and he heard the sounds of agonizing screams that were unbearable to hear;

he covered his ears and eyes, prostrated himself, and begged for release, feeling as though his heart were breaking and blood flowing from his mouth. When the messengers led him back, the King said, "Since you have eaten the flesh, you may not return empty-handed.
He immediately ordered five long nails to be driven into his head, hands, and feet, causing him excruciating pain. From [this point]...

This man was devoted to the recitation of the sutras and abstained from eating meat. Later, while on official business at a post station, he suddenly dreamed of a woman in green clothing who begged for his mercy.
He inquired of the station clerk, "What provisions are there for food? The clerk replied, "I see a sheep prepared;
it is very fat and tender. He went to it and said, "It is a blue ewe. Wenruo declared, "I do not eat meat," and subsequently ransomed it and set it free (from the *Baoying ji*).
Zhao Wenchang, a Vice Director of the Grand Court of the Imperial Guards during the eleventh year of the Kaihuang era of the Sui dynasty, suddenly died of a violent illness.
Only his heart remained slightly warm, so his family did not dare to enshroud him. Later, he returned to life and recounted: "When I first died, someone led me to the realm of King Yama."
The king asked, "What meritorious deeds have you performed throughout your life? Chang replied, "My family is poor and lacks the means to cultivate merit;
I have done nothing but single-mindedly recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Upon hearing these words, the king joined his palms, bowed his head, and praised him, saying, "Excellent!
Since you uphold the *Prajñā*, your merit is truly vast. The king then dispatched an attendant to lead him away.
Wenchang went into the sutra repository and took out a copy of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

Wenchang walked westward for five or six li and saw several dozen buildings that were extremely magnificent. Within them, scriptures filled every space; they were bound in golden rollers and precious cases, exquisitely adorned and of fine quality.
Wenchang joined his palms and closed his eyes, then drew a single scroll at random from his hand. Upon opening it to read, it was indeed the *Vajracchedikā*.

Wen Chang held the *Prajñāpāramitā* Sūtra up to the King’s presence and ordered one person to hold the scroll to the west while he stood to the east facing the scripture, reciting it without omitting a single character.
The King was greatly delighted and immediately released Wen Chang to return home. He then had Wen Chang led out through the south gate;
at the gatehead, he saw Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou inside a side room by the gate, wearing three layers of iron shackles.
The Emperor summoned Chang and said, "You are a native of my own country; you have come here for a time, and I wish to speak with you.
Chang Wen then prostrated himself. The Emperor asked, "Do you recognize me? Chang Wen replied, "Your servant formerly served as a guard to Your Majesty.
Emperor Wu said, "Since you were my former minister, now that you are returning home, go to the Emperor of Sui and tell him of my various [intentions]."
"Your sins are grave; you wish to distinguish yourself, yet the offense of rejecting the Buddha's Dharma is so heavy that it cannot be avoided.
I hope you will perform some small meritorious deed for me, so that by this blessing and protection, I may escape hell. Chang accepted his words and departed.
Upon exiting through the southern gate, he saw a large pit of excrement with a person whose hair was protruding from above. Chang questioned him, and the man being led there replied, "This is..."
The Qin general Bai Qi was detained here; his crimes were not yet fully expiated when Chang arrived at his home and was able to survive.

He subsequently reported this matter to the Emperor, who ordered that a tax be levied on the population to recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* for the sake of Emperor Wu of the Northern Zhou.
A great offering was made for three days, and the account of these events was recorded and included in the Sui Shu (History of the Sui Dynasty) (*from the Fayuan zhulin*).
Regarding the scholar of Xinpan County:
in Xinpan County, Yizhou, forty li to the west, lies Wangli Village. During the Sui dynasty, there lived a scholar there surnamed Xun.
He was a skilled calligrapher who concealed his traces; no one could discern them.

Once, in the air to the east of a village, he wrote the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* on all four sides for several days until it was complete, saying, "This sutra is intended for the devas to recite.
People were initially unaware of it. Later, during a thunderstorm, a young cowherd stood at the place where the sutra had been written and remained unsprinkled by the rain.
The ground was damp for a space of about one *zhang*. When it cleared, the villagers found this strange.
Thereafter, whenever it rained, young children would constantly gather there, yet their clothes would not get wet. During the Wude era of the Tang dynasty, a strange monk said to the villagers:
In the air above this site, there is the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. The devas have established jeweled canopies above it to cover it, so that it may not be lightly violated.
Since then, railings have been erected on all four sides to prevent humans and livestock from treading upon it.

Whenever the day of the fast arrives, villagers from the surrounding areas come to present offerings to the Buddha; the sound of celestial music is constantly heard, resonating through the vast void as it fills the space with its rich harmony.
Ear (from the *Sambao Gantong Ji*; the surname Xun is also written as Gou).
Kuai Wu’an of the Sui dynasty was a native of Cai Prefecture. He possessed great physical strength and was skilled with the bow and arrow; he frequently hunted tigers. Once, at Mount Song...
Nan was extremely violent. He went to shoot him, and as they gradually reached a deep mountain, there suddenly appeared a strange creature with hands like those of a wild man.
It opened a large beast’s hide and threw it over Wuan’s body, then pushed him down into a ravine. When he rose up, he had already become a large beast.
Terrified and trembling with fear, he did not know what to do. Suddenly hearing the sound of a bell, he realized it was a monastic residence and went there to seek help.

Indeed, he saw a monk reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. He immediately closed his eyes and prostrated himself. The monk stroked his head with his hand, and suddenly there was a loud explosion;
his head had already burst open. Wú'ān then emerged from within it and related the previous events in detail. Furthermore, [the monk] patted him...

The back opened as he moved his hand, and once he emerged, his entire body and all his clothing were intact; there were a few hairs from a large beast, which were likely those adhering to the ulcer from his previous cauterization.
From this point on, he left the household life and devoted himself exclusively to upholding the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* (from the *Baoying ji*).

Muyantong of the Sui dynasty was a person who recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* with great devotion, performing ten recitations daily. When Li Mi’s rebellion broke out, Muyantong served as the magistrate of Wulao.
The local people intended to kill him so that he might join the banners of the righteous cause. Muyantong learned of this beforehand and consequently fled to the city.
Below, bandits drew their swords to pursue him. Upon reaching a deep ravine, he was pressed in extremity and leaped into it.
It was as if someone had caught his right arm and placed him upon a flat rock; he suffered no injury at all. A voice spoke from the air, saying: "This is due to your recitation of the sutras."
He was thus able to return home. The arm he had received emitted a wondrous fragrance that did not dissipate for several days.
Later, he rose to the rank of Regional Inspector (Fangbo) and lived until the age of ninety-odd before passing away. (From the *Baoying ji*).
Du Zhiliang was a man of the Sui dynasty. During the Renshou era, he served as a military aide (*chamjun*) to Prince Liang of Han.

Later, when Liang raised troops in rebellion at Bingzhou and was defeated, Zhiliang and his subordinates were all imprisoned. Terrified and distressed, Zhiliang wept day and night; suddenly, one night, he dreamed.
A monk said, "If you simply recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, this calamity can be overcome. At dawn, he took the scripture and practiced its recitation with single-minded devotion.
When the executioners led him and the others to their deaths, Huiliang was among them; as they were being executed, all those who chanted [the sutra] died.
Only the name of Wuliang was not recorded. Those in charge of the records were all punished for their negligence, though they were soon pardoned by a general amnesty.
During the Xianqing era, he died while serving as the Prefect of Huangzhou (as recorded in the *Baoying ji*).
Murong Wencè, a man of the Sui dynasty, regularly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and abstained from wine and meat. In the seventh year of the Daye era, he died suddenly;
three days later, he revived and said: "At first, I saw two ghosts who, holding official documents, pursued me to the gate of a city. Looking back, it was extremely—"

The atmosphere was solemn. After traveling four or five *li*, they saw a palace. The King sat upon the throne, surrounded by a retinue of guards; monks and followers from the four quarters were beyond counting.
The envoy entered to have an audience, with the written memorial (*wen-ce*) held last. One by one, [the officials] were questioned regarding the good and evil deeds committed during their lifetimes.
They were ordered to stand facing east and west, and then the names from the memorial were called out. When it came to the question, "What good deeds did you perform? he replied, "Since my youth..."
He was reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Upon hearing this, the king joined his palms and sighed in praise, saying, "The merit of this is truly vast.

He then released him to return home. Suddenly, he saw two monks holding torches and leading the way; he immediately grasped the corner of their *kāṣāya* robes and questioned them. The monks said, "It is because you uphold this sūtra that we have come to protect you.
You may follow the light of our candles. They then departed through the city gate. The monks asked, "Do you know the location of hell? and pointed toward one place.
The great city gate said, "This is it. Zé could not bear to look and begged to depart quickly. The two monks then led him away.
Upon reaching the road, there was a cross-wall blocking the way; the monk struck it with his staff, and it opened immediately, saying, "You may go this way.
Thereupon he was restored to life (from the *Bàoyìng jì*).
Liu Jian was the Sima of Xingzhou during the Tang dynasty. In the tenth year of the Daye era of the Sui dynasty, he served as the Superintendent of Qiyang Palace in Qizhou.
By the first year of the Yining era, he was imprisoned in the Dali Si for being falsely accused. With a sincere heart, Liu Jian recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

There were two sheets of scripture remaining that had not yet been recited. Unaware of this, he fell asleep. In a dream, he was told by a Brahmin monk, "Donor, you ought to recite the scriptures until they are complete;
then you shall be released. Sengjian suddenly awoke and continued his recitation with diligent perseverance.

After two days, an imperial decree was suddenly issued summoning him to the court hall, where he was granted a pardon. Furthermore, on another occasion, while Sengjian was reciting the scriptures at night during the third watch, he suddenly heard a voice.
A rare fragrance wafted through and filled the entire residence, continuing without ceasing until dawn; this was surely brought about by spiritual resonance.
By the time of his death, Sengjian had recited the sutras more than five thousand times (from the Fayuan zhulin).
Xiao Yu, Xiao Yu.

He was the great-grandson of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty and the son of Prince Gui of Liang. After the fall of the Liang, he entered the Sui dynasty, where he served as Grand Secretary (Zhongshu Ling) and was enfeoffed as the Duke of Song.
His daughter was the Empress Dowager of Emperor Yang. He was a devout believer in the Buddha-dharma and constantly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. [Discourse follows.]
The campaign against Koguryo did not accord with the Emperor’s wishes, and he was greatly incensed. He placed Yu under house arrest together with He Ruo-bi and Gao Jing, intending to execute them.
Yu remained in his quarters for eight days, reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* seven hundred times. The following day, his shackles suddenly fell off of their own accord.

The guards turned pale with alarm; they re-applied the fetters and led him before the palace. The Emperor alone granted clemency to Yu and the other two, who were then severely punished. Consequently—

There are eighteen accounts of miraculous responses concerning the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. He then constructed a precious stupa, enshrining the scripture and sandalwood within it, making it three feet high.
Thereupon, a brass image suddenly appeared in his courtyard; he enshrined it within the stupa and obtained one hundred grains of śarīra.
In the eleventh year of the Zhenguan era, he beheld the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, who drifted slowly toward the west (from the *Baoying ji*).
Zhao Wenxin was a native of Suzhou in Tang China. In the first year of the Zhenguan era, he died suddenly; three days later, he revived.
He recounted that at the time of his death, he had been driven along by a crowd of people, accompanied by ten fellow travelers, until they reached King Yama.
Among them was a monk whom the King first asked: "Master, what meritorious deeds have you cultivated during your life? The Master replied:

"Since my birth, this poor monk has done nothing but recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Upon hearing these words, the King suddenly rose in alarm, joined his palms in reverence, and praised him, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! Since you truly recite the *Prajñā*, you shall surely ascend to heaven. For what reason [is this]?"
"I have come here by mistake. Before he had finished speaking, a heavenly robe suddenly descended, and it led the Master up into the sky.

The King then called out to the man from Suizhou, who came forward and said, "What meritorious deeds did you perform during your lifetime? The man replied, "Throughout my life, I have not read Buddhist scriptures;
I have only been fond of the collected literary works of Yu Xin. The King said, "Yu Xin is a person of great sin."
The man said, "I see this person suffering. Do you recognize Yu Xin? He replied, "Although I have read his writings, I do not know the man.
The King immediately ordered Yu Xin to be brought forward. When he was seen, he had the body of a tortoise. The King then ordered him to be led away.
After a short while, he returned in human form and said, "Because during my life I took pleasure in composing literary works and recklessly cited the Buddha..."
He had intermixed secular texts with the sutras and slandered the Buddha-dharma, claiming it was inferior to the teachings of Confucius and Laozi.
Now he undergoes the retribution for his sins, suffering in the form of a tortoise. After this man was revived, he recounted these events in detail. Many people in Suzhou were fond of hunting;
upon hearing what he said, they all took it to heart as a warning, forever severing their karmic habit of killing. Each gave rise to a sincere mind and undertook to uphold the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
If [this practice] continues without ceasing to this day (as recorded in the *Fayuan zhulin*).
Liu Bi, a native of the Tang dynasty, served as the County Magistrate of Jiangnan during the first year of the Zhenguan era. One day, a strange bird suddenly appeared at his residence.
It perched and cried atop a tree in front of him. The local people said that the place where this bird alights brings ill omen.

Upon hearing this, Sengbi was struck with fear and desired to cultivate merit, yet he did not know which practice would be most superior. During the night, he dreamed of a monk who praised the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* exclusively and commanded him to recite it one hundred times.
Upon waking, he followed these instructions and immediately recited it until he reached the hundredth repetition. Suddenly, a great wind arose from—

[The wind] came from the northeast. It uprooted this tree and hurled it across the house, far out into the alleyway. At the spot where it was pulled up, there was a pit in the earth measuring one zhang and five chi in length and breadth.
Observing the direction from which the violent wind had come, the small branches and delicate leaves all bent and swayed along with the wind;
when the wind ceased, they rose back up as before. Thus one knows that the power of the sutras is inconceivable (from the *Fayuan zhulin*).
Yuan Zhitong of the Tang dynasty was a native of Tianshui. He regularly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. At the age of twenty, he was conscripted as a soldier.
While fleeing from a defeated army into steep and dangerous ravines, he went for days without food; yet he perceived two youths approaching, carrying bowls full of rice which they offered to him.
Zhitong bowed in greeting, and suddenly he vanished. After he had finished eating, he did not feel hungry for several days.
Later, he was able to return to his home village. In the eighth year of the Zhenguan era, he fell ill and died; two days later, he revived and said, "I was led before the King.

The King asked about my good deeds during my life. I replied, 'I constantly recited the Diamond Sūtra. The King was greatly pleased and said, 'Have him sent out first,' and so I returned to life" (from the *Baoying ji*).

Wei Qiqin of the Tang dynasty, Wei Qiqin by name. In his youth, he recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. He served as a General of the Household (*zhonglang jiang*) and followed the army to campaign against Liaodong.
He was captured by Goguryeo. During the Zhenguan era, when Emperor Taizong campaigned against Liaodong, Qiqin [saw] from afar the imperial troops at night... and so forth.
He went out to throw it away, but in the darkness he did not know the way. Thereupon, he focused his mind on reciting the sutra; suddenly, he saw a torch leading the way before him.
Kechin followed the fire and eventually reached the Han army (from the *Baoying ji*).
Shen Jiahui of the Tang dynasty served as a Proofreader (Jiàoshūláng) during the Zhenguan period. On account of certain affairs, he was assigned to Lanzhou.

His longing to return home was so intense that every morning and evening he would regularly face east and bow toward Mount Tai, praying to be allowed to return alive. After more than two hundred days had passed, during the Yonghui era...
On the third day of the tenth month in the sixth year, at night, he saw two youths whose appearance and attire were most elegant.
They said they were the sons of the Lord of Mount Tai. Because the Lord was ashamed that the Master had been paying him homage morning and evening, he had sent them to welcome him.
Jia Hui asked, "Mount Tai is over three thousand *li* away; how can you go there? The youths replied, "Master, close your eyes; do not worry about the distance. Immediately—
Following his instructions, they arrived in an instant. The palace was magnificent and grand; the youth led them inside to pay their respects to the Lord of the Prefecture.
He immediately invited them into a private chamber, where they sat facing one another in conversation and laughter. He knew everything, saying to Jia Hui:
"When a person commits evil, if they are not executed by others while alive, they will certainly be seized and punished as a ghost after death; there is no way to seek fortune or evade this."

This is an exemption. If one recites the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* once daily, then all ten thousand sins will be extinguished, and the officials of the underworld will be unable to detain them.
Furthermore, it was said: "The former Magistrate committed an offense, and the Celestial Bureau has demoted him.
I, Liu Jiahui, also dare not inquire about other matters. Once, while playing *shuanglu* (a game of dice) with Jiahui, we also set out wine and delicacies; Jiahui rose from his seat..."

In the hall, he looked toward Guzang. Murong Renguī stood holding his ceremonial tablet and sat upright, saying, "The Prefect’s summons has reached me here sixty days ago, yet I have not received any instructions. Jiahui sat up and addressed him;
the Prefect then ordered Renguī to be summoned inside and said to him, "Under your jurisdiction, there was a woman named Āzhào who was unjustly tortured to death by the County Magistrate. Āzhào—"

He came to lodge a complaint and consequently mistakenly summoned the Duke. In front of the hall was a basin of water; the Duke ordered him to wash his face and then sent a young boy to escort him back.
Jiahui also took his leave, but the Duke again ordered two of his sons to see him off. He remained at Mount Tai for a total of twenty-eight days.
His family merely perceived his spirit to be clouded and dim; once he returned, he was as he had been before.
Jia Hui discussed Ren Gui with Zhao Chiman, one of the many *changshi*, and had him verify this, finding it to be exactly the same.
From then on, he constantly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and, encountering a general amnesty, was able to return home (*from the Baoying ji*).
Lu Huaisu of Wu Commandery during the Tang dynasty: In the twentieth year of the Zhenguan era, a fire broke out and his residence was consumed by flames, vanishing along with the smoke;
only the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* remained. Even the case and the binding scrolls were destroyed, leaving only the scripture itself.
The characters remained exactly as they were before. Those who heard of this could not help but be struck with wonder and admiration. Huaisu was the elder brother of Xu Renze’s wife;
Renze witnessed it with his own eyes and frequently spoke of it to others (from the *Mingbao ji*).
Sima Qiaoqing of Henei was a *sili* (Court Rectifier) of the Ministry of Justice during the Tang dynasty. By nature he was pure and prudent, and possessed noble aspirations and conduct.

During the Yonghui era, he served as the *sihu cao* (Assistant Administrator of the Household Registry) of Yangzhou. Upon the death of his mother, he observed the mourning rites with such emaciation that he became a mere skeleton; he even pierced his own flesh to draw blood for copying the *Golden Light Sutra*.
The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* in two fascicles. Not long after, two stalks of *zhicao* (mushroom) grew by the side of the [textual] chamber.

On the ninth day, they reached a length of one chi and eight cun; their stems were green and their caps were crimson. Each day they exuded one *sheng* of juice. When eaten, its flavor was as sweet as honey. Once harvested, it would grow back again.
Qiao Qing and several of his colleagues all witnessed this event with their own eyes (*from Fayuan zhulin*).
During the Xianqing era of the Tang dynasty, there was a man named Sun Shou from Pingzhou. While out hunting along the seashore, he encountered a wildfire that consumed all the grasses and trees;
only a single thicket of lush vegetation remained unburnt. Suspecting there might be a hidden beast within the grass, he proceeded to probe it with fire.
The fire ultimately failed to burn it. Sun Shou found this most strange; he entered the grass to investigate and discovered a case containing the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
Beside it lay the corpse of a deceased monk, whose complexion remained unchanged and who had not been consumed by the spreading flames. It was evidently due to this that the fire did not spread.
Only then did he realize that scriptures and images are beyond the comprehension of ordinary beings. Sun Shou recounted this himself (*from the Fayuan zhulin*).
Li Guan was a native of Longxi during the Tang dynasty. During the Xianqing era, he resided in Yingyang.

Upon the death of his father, he drew blood from his own body to transcribe one scroll each of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*. Thereafter, a constant and extraordinary phenomenon occurred within his courtyard.
The fragrance was exceptionally rich and intense; even those in neighboring houses could constantly smell it, and there were none who did not praise it.
Xu Ling, the Magistrate of Zhongshan County, while passing through Zhengzhou, visited an acquaintance there and related this matter in full detail (from the Fayuan zhulin).
Lady Doulu was the wife of Duke Dou of the Chen State during the Tang dynasty. She was of the Doulu clan and was the elder sister of Duke Rui, Dou Kuan.

The lady believed deeply in the retribution of sin and merit and constantly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. When she had not yet finished more than a single sheet of paper from the scroll, she suddenly developed a headache; by nightfall, it had become even worse.
"It is so. The lady thought to herself, "If I die now, I shall not be able to complete this scripture. She wished to rise and recite it, so she told her maidservant to light a candle;
however, the lamps were all extinguished, and the maid returned empty-handed. The lady sighed with even deeper regret.

Suddenly, she saw a torch in the kitchen that gradually ascended the hall steps and entered her bedchamber directly, hovering about three feet above the ground without anyone holding it, its radiance brilliant.

If it was during the day, the lady would be filled with wonder and joy; she would take up the scripture and recite it. After a short while, when the family members struck flint to produce fire, the light of the candle would immediately extinguish itself.
From then on, she recited it five times every day as her regular practice. Later, when Lord Rui was about to die, the lady went to visit him.
The lord said to the lady, "By the merit of your recitation of the scripture, you shall live for a hundred years and be reborn in a good realm."
Furthermore, when this lady reached the age of eighty, she passed away without illness (as recorded in the *Fayuan zhulin*).
Regarding the nun Xiuxing:
in the first year of the Longshuo era of the Tang dynasty, at Jingfu Temple in Luozhou, the nun Xiuxing had a servant boy in her quarters.

Wu Wuniang died and subsequently practiced the Way. A spirit seat was established for her, and after more than a month had passed, her elder sister and younger brother suddenly heard moaning from the spirit seat during the night.
At first, the younger brother was greatly terrified, but later he questioned her.
She replied, "In my lifetime, I ate meat at the monastery; because of this, I am suffering great agony. Upon my body there are..."
She had a sore and, fearing it might soil the bedding, said to her younger brother, "You should take plenty of ash and place it upon the bed.

The brother followed her words; after the ash was placed, he looked upon the bed and saw that there was a great deal of pus and blood. She spoke to him again, saying, "I am too ill to sew clothes. You are wearing very tattered rags;
you should bring some cloth, and I will make a shirt and socks for you. The brother then placed the cloth upon the funeral couch.
After one night, it was completed. He then said to his sister, "When I was a child and fell ill, I killed a crab and applied its juice to my wound, which allowed me to recover.
Now I have entered the Hell of the Blade Forest; within my flesh, seven broken blades are visible.

I pray that you, out of compassion, will perform meritorious deeds on my behalf to rescue me. His sister, being pressed by urgency, found it difficult to prepare the offerings immediately; she could only carry them with her.
"Clothing is of no benefit to the deceased, yet it has not yet been ruined; please take it for use. Before his sister could reply, he said, "The child shall take it himself.
After a long while, he spoke again: "The clothing has been here on the bed since it was brought. His sister went to look and found it was the very shroud used for the enshrouding.
She then sent it to Master Bǎoxiàn at Jìngtǔ Temple to commission the copying of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*.
In the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, every time he finished copying one fascicle, he would announce, "One blade has been drawn.
When he had finished copying all seven fascicles, he said, "The seven blades have all been drawn forth; now, sustained by the merit of my blessings, I shall immediately go to take rebirth.
He then departed to weep in farewell with his elder sister and younger brother. This was related by the monk Zhizheng of Jingtu Monastery, as recounted by Shen Xuangfa of Wuxing.
This is also the same [as in the *Mingbao ji*].
Chen Wenda was a native of Qi County, Zizhou during the Tang dynasty. He regularly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, vowing that its merit might be shared with his deceased parents.
There were eighty-four thousand scrolls [of this scripture], accompanied by many auspicious signs. For those who recited it for others, all hardships and calamities were avoided.
Chen Yue of Tongsan County was once summoned by the authorities of the underworld. He saw a platform being constructed underground and asked about it;
they replied, "This is the Prajñā Platform, awaiting Chen Wenda. Such was the reverence shown to him by the authorities of the underworld (from *Fayuan zhulin*).
Gao Zhi was the grandson of Gao Yingzhi, the Minister of Works (Puye) of the Sui dynasty.

In the second year of the Longshuo era of the Tang dynasty, as he was exiting the Shunyi Gate of Chang’an, he suddenly encountered two men riding horses who said, “The King summons Zhi. Zhi refused to go with them, nor did he realize they were ghosts. They compelled him.
He spurred his horse to avoid it, but was again driven and crowded forward. Zhi had an elder brother who was a monk at Huadu Monastery;

wishing to go inside the temple, he reached the gate when a ghost blocked him, refusing to let him enter. Zhi struck the ghost with a single punch. The ghost grew enraged and immediately dragged him off his horse, saying, "This man is a great rogue and a brute.
Zhi’s body then fell to the ground, and he immediately lost consciousness. The monks of the monastery then ordered him to be carried inside.
The elder brother’s monastery. At dawn the next day, he revived and said: "At first, I followed the two messengers and saw the King. The King said, 'It is not yet fitting for you to come here;

you once slandered the Buddha-dharma, so let me have you undergo its punishment in this life. He ordered his attendants to pull out my tongue and plow it with a plowshare, yet I suffered no injury at all.
The King asked his chief official, 'What merit does this man possess to be such? He replied, 'He once recited..."

The King praised the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and immediately ordered him to be released and sent back. While conversing with his guests, he suddenly collapsed in a faint, appearing as if he were swallowing something;
a single white pulse appeared beneath his throat and flowed into his abdomen. This occurred three times.
When people questioned him about it, he said, "In my youth, I stole temple fruit. The underworld authorities punished me by ordering me to swallow iron pellets. Later, he served as an official...
Attendant Guards: Devoted exclusively to the practice of reciting scriptures (from the *Baoying ji*).
Bai Renzhe of the Tang dynasty served as the District Magistrate of Zhuyang in Guozhou during the Longshuo era. He was dispatched to transport rice to Liaodong; while crossing the sea—

They encountered a storm, and as they looked in the four directions, all was dark and gloomy. Renzhi was filled with anxiety and fear; he urgently recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* until he had completed three hundred repetitions.
Suddenly, as if in a dream, he saw a Brahman monk who said to him, "Because you have recited the true scripture, I have come to save you.
In an instant, the wind subsided, and all eighty-odd people were safely delivered. (From the *Baoying ji*).
Doux De-xuan.
During the Linde era, while serving as a high official on a mission to Yangzhou, he crossed the Huai River.
His boat had already moved dozens of paces from the shore when he saw a man on the bank who was haggard and emaciated; holding a small bundle, the man sat upon the ground. De-xuan...
He said, "The sun is about to set and there is no boat to ferry us across. He immediately ordered the man to carry him.

Midway through the stream, he noticed the man’s hungry expression and gave him some rice before they reached the other side. When De Xuan mounted his horse and departed, the man followed right behind him for several li.
De Xuan, finding this strange, asked, "Where do you intend to go now? The man replied, "I am not a human; I am a messenger of the ghosts. I am going now to—"
In Yangzhou, he pursued the Grand Administrator Dou. He asked, "What is your name? Dou replied, "My name is Dexuan. Dexuan was struck with alarm and fear;

he dismounted from his horse and prostrated himself, saying, "I am that very man. Shedding tears and sobbing, he begged for counsel. The ghost said, "I am deeply grateful that you gave me passage and even provided me with food.
Furthermore, I shall release you. You must immediately recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* one thousand times; I shall come to repay your kindness. When the month arrived...
In other sutras, once the required number was complete, the ghost would indeed arrive; it was said that since the quota was met, there was no need for further concern.
Nevertheless, one must ultimately go along with them to see the King. At this, De-huan went to his pillow and passed away. After one night, he revived and said:
"At first, I followed the messenger into a palace city. The messenger said, 'Sir, wait here for a moment; I shall first announce your arrival to the King. The messenger then entered."
Behind a screen, he later heard the King speaking from afar, saying, "You conspired with him to leak my secret. He was consequently flogged thirty times.
The messenger came out, baring his back to show it to the official, and said, "I have received the flogging. De-huan thanked him repeatedly for his shame.
He was then led inside, where he saw a man dressed in purple robes. Descending the steps, the man bowed to him and said, "You have performed a great service."
"Your virtue has not yet been matched. I request that you return and fall back into the pit; thus, you shall live. Thereupon, he was restored to life.
The messenger arrived again and said, "I have not yet eaten from hunger; give me whatever wealth I beg for. When asked about his future official rank, he replied, "Memorize this well.

From then on, he was appointed as Director of the Palace Interior (*Dianzhongjian*), followed by Grand Minister of Rites (*Dasixian*), followed by Attendant-in-Ordinary to the Crown Prince (*Taizhongyun*), and finally Director of the Bureau of Personnel (*Siyuan*).

He was appointed as the Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Taichangbo), followed by the Left Chancellor. When he reached the age of sixty-four, having finished speaking, he took his leave, saying, "I shall not come here again.
Subsequently, everything occurred exactly as he had said. (From the *Baoying ji*).
Song Yilun of the Tang dynasty was serving as the Chief Scribe for the Prince of Guo during the Linde era. He died suddenly and did not revive until three days later.

He said that he had been summoned to see the Prince. The Prince said, "You once killed dogs, rabbits, and pigeons; now you have been brought before me for judgment. Your allotted lifespan has reached its end. However...
I recently saw your master, who said that by reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, you would not only extinguish your sins but also extend your lifespan.
I have now released you; can you henceforth refrain from consuming alcohol and meat and continue to uphold this honored scripture? Yilun bowed in thanks and replied, "I can.
He then saw a monk on a bed inside the hall, appearing to be fifty or sixty years old and wearing a patched robe (*kaṣāya*); Yilun immediately prostrated himself before him.
The monk said, "I am your teacher, which is why I have come to save you; you may follow the King's words. Yilun replied, "Yes.
The King ordered him to go with the messengers to observe hell. Upon entering the first location, he saw rows of large cauldrons with fires burning beneath them.
People were being boiled in cauldrons; their cries of agony were heart-rending beyond measure. They entered another place where there was an iron bed, exceedingly wide.

A person lay upon it, scorched and blackened until their features could no longer be distinguished. Looking westward, they saw three figures standing there, withered and dark, appearing somewhat like women.
They knelt before Yilun and said, "We have not been able to eat for several hundred years. Yilun—
He replied, "I myself have nothing; what could I give you? You must enter another hell.

He then said to the messenger, "It was so hot that I feared my family would find me and take me away, so I left. He walked southwest for several dozen paces, then called out, "I have no document; I fear the gatekeeper will not let me out.
He subsequently obtained three lines of vermilion writing, though he did not recognize a single character. The gatekeeper indeed questioned him, and he looked at them.

Liao Fuchu was restored to life (from the *Baoying ji*). Li Gang, the Minister of War of the Tang dynasty, fell ill and died suddenly; however, his heart remained warm. After three days, he revived and said: ... [The remainder of the passage follows] ...he saw a great hall where a man sat upon a high seat. He asked, "Who are you? The man replied, "I am the King of Hell. He further asked, "What offense did I commit that I have come here? The King of Hell replied, "You have committed no offense.

You were merely summoned to see the workings of retribution. Now you may return. Li Gang then departed. Upon reaching the gate, he saw a man with a sword at his side who asked him, "Did you see anything extraordinary? Li Gang replied, "I saw nothing. The man struck him with his sword, and he immediately revived. He told his family everything he had seen. Later, when he was again summoned by the King of Hell, he saw the same man with the sword at his side. The man struck him again, and he revived once more. He told his family what he had seen this time as well. From then on, he never again went to the underworld. His son, Li Zhongyuan, later became a monk and attained the Way. Li Gang was the Minister of War of the Tang dynasty. He fell ill and died suddenly; only his heart remained warm. After three days, he revived and spoke thus.
He saw a man being led away for interrogation. The Great General ordered him to sit and summoned a desk. Upon inspection, it was said, "We have mistakenly pursued you, sir.
After a short while, a jailer brought forward a tray containing several iron balls. He then carried in a cauldron and set it down in the courtyard;
fire spontaneously erupted from beneath the cauldron, and molten copper boiled and surged within it. The iron balls were as red as fire. The jailer stepped forward.
The plate was offered by the general to Wang Gang. Fearing for his life, Gang said he was full. The general swallowed it; once it had entered his mouth, his entire body became transparently radiant.
He then drank molten copper, whereupon flames erupted from his body. In the space of a single breath, he swallowed it all.

After a long while, he returned to his normal state. Gang then stepped forward and questioned him. He replied, "In the underworld there are no other delicacies; there is only this. Thus, I simply sucked it up."
He ate it; had he not done so, he would have been consumed by a fierce fire in an instant, suffering far worse than this.

He did nothing but transcribe ten volumes of Buddhist scriptures and recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* one thousand times. The official did not come again, and I too departed from that place.
When the ridge once more grew back, everything was exactly as we had agreed upon. [This account appears in the *Baoying ji*.]

Wang Tuo was a *guoyi* (fruitful commander) of the Eagle-Flight Commandery (*Yingyang Fu*). Having fallen ill, he subsequently abstained from pungent meats and resolved his mind [upon the Dharma], reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* five times daily.
Later, he contracted a malarial fever and saw a host of ghosts approaching. Wang Tuo immediately and urgently recited the sutra; upon hearing it, the ghosts...

The ghost retreated and called out from afar, "The King has ordered you to be pursued; cease reciting the sutra for now. Dharmatā immediately stopped. The ghosts all moved forward, and Dharmatā fell into a stupor, on the verge of death.
After a short while, he saw another ghost come and say, "The King has granted a temporary reprieve of six months for the person who recites the sutra.
Upon awakening, he then devoted himself single-mindedly to the recitation, never ceasing day or night. Although the six months had passed, the ghosts did not appear.
Later, at night, he heard a voice in the air calling out: "By virtue of your merit in upholding this sutra, you shall live to the age of ninety.
It was exactly as he had been told (from the *Baoying ji*).

Wang Lingwang, a native of Tang, had recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* since his youth. While returning to Qiongzhou, he encountered a fierce beast on an extremely perilous path by the stream.
Overcome with intense terror, he hurriedly recited the true scripture. The beast stared at him intently, then trailed its tail away, dripping with saliva.
Man Di once served as the Administrative Assistant (Panshi) of Anzhou. While crossing the Yangtze River, a violent wind arose at night;
several hundred hired boats following one another all sank, yet only the boat of Ling Wang remained intact. He later died as the Magistrate of Qiao in Bozhou (as recorded in the *Baoying ji*).

Jing swore an oath, saying, "If you do not marry me, once I become a ghost, I will certainly bring disaster upon you. Later, she returned to marry Hui. Hui... [was killed]. Wang Shi then took an oath, saying, "I shall surely bring disaster upon him. Subsequently, Hui’s younger brother died suddenly; his corpse was swollen and his mouth emitted a foul odor. When Wang Shi went to the side of the bed to wail, the corpse suddenly sat up and spoke, saying, "It was you who brought this disaster upon me.
