Jing was the Magistrate of Renshou in Lingzhou. After he died, Wang dreamed of him; upon waking, she became pregnant.
She carried the fetus for seventeen months without giving birth. Filled with anxiety and fear, Wang resolved to recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* day and night without ceasing.
Jing’s spirit was forever severed from her, and the ghostly fetus dissolved as well. From then on, she recited it seven times every day (*Record of Retribution*).
He Jiong of Tang was serving as the Magistrate of Wude in Huai Prefecture at the beginning of the Tianshou era. He constantly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

Once, when he reached Heyang, the river rose and the bridge collapsed; it was already evening, and people were scrambling onto boats. The bank was far away and they had not yet reached safety when they were about to be submerged. Jiong was terrified, and moreover—
He urgently recited a sutra. In a short while, they reached the shore; he encountered hanging reeds and climbed them to escape, while more than eighty other people drowned (from the *Baoying ji*).

Zhang Xuansu was a native of Luoyang during the Tang dynasty. In his youth, he maintained the practice of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. At the beginning of the Tianguan era, he served as the magistrate of Huangmei.

When his family encountered a calamity, it was dispelled by the mere power of his mindfulness. At the age of seventy, he fell ill; suddenly, flowered canopies hung in the sky, whereupon he bathed himself.
He bathed, bid farewell to his family, and suddenly passed away (as recorded in the *Baoying ji*).
Li Qiuyi was a man of the Tang dynasty who delighted in hawks, dogs, and hunting. In the first year of the Wansui Tongtian era, he served as the governor of Gaoyou in Yangzhou.
The Assistant Minister suddenly died one day from a violent illness. He saw two men come to pursue him; one of them identified himself as surnamed Duan.
At that time, there were over a hundred others being pursued together—men all wearing cangues and women bound hand and foot behind their backs. Qiu was placed first in the procession, shackled.
After traveling about ten li, they saw several dozen large locust trees with horse troughs beneath them. Duan said, "This is the Great Deity of the Five Paths."
Whenever he patrols among humans to observe their merits and transgressions, he halts his horse here. Qiu Yi suddenly realized that his life had ended and he had arrived at the King’s gate.
Duan Zhi pointed to an official and said, "This man is surnamed Jiao and named Ce; he was your original head. Consequently, he was led into the presence of the King.
The King said, "How could you endure such cruelty and lack of kinship? You took pleasure in killing the lives of others for your own enjoyment. In a moment, you shall see those whom you killed."
The birds and beasts all spoke in human voices, saying, "Please grant us a resolution at once. Jiao Ce stepped forward and said, "Qiu Yi has not yet deserved death.
The King asked, "What meritorious deeds did he perform? He replied, "He only once transcribed one scroll of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

The King immediately joined his palms and said, "In the netherworld, the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* is called the supreme merit. Since you were able to transcribe it, your fortune is no small matter. Immediately—
He ordered Jiao Ce to lead him toward the scripture repository. Upon reaching a magnificent jewel palace filled with all manner of scriptures, Qiu Yi drew out a single scroll at random;
it was indeed the very scripture he had composed. When he returned and saw this, the King realized that his composition was authentic.

He then summoned the living beings he had killed and ordered them to offer sincere apologies, granting them the opportunity to perform meritorious deeds. Following the King’s command, Qiu Yi vowed to transcribe the *Vajracchedikā*.

The sutras totaled one hundred fascicles. When the assembly had finished dispersing in joy, the King said, "Release him. Jiao Ce led him out through the city gate and said, "You have exerted yourself to such an extent;
how can you not be rewarded? Qiu Yi offered three hundred thousand coins, but [Ce] would not accept them, saying, "I shall have twenty sets of the sutras made for you.
Upon reaching a pit, Ce pushed him in; he was then restored to life inside the coffin, hearing only the sound of weeping.
Three days had passed when he cried out in alarm; people arrived and broke open the coffin, whereupon he rose up. Within ten days, he completed the transcription of twenty fascicles of the sutra.

Jiao Ce came to offer his thanks and departed after delivering his message. Soon thereafter, the hundred fascicles were also finished. The Regional Inspector of Yangzhou submitted a report on these matters to the throne.
By imperial decree, he was promoted to the fifth rank and appointed as the Pacification Commissioner of Jiazhou (as recorded in the *Baoying ji*).
Yu Chang (of the Tang dynasty) served as the Registrar of Pingzhou during the reign of Empress Wu. Every time it reached the first watch after nightfall, he would gasp for breath.
His perspiration ceased and he recovered after the second watch. His wife, Lady Liu, was about to summon a physician when Xuanchang secretly said, "I have no other suffering;

it is simply that by day I manage the affairs of the judicial office, and by night I adjudicate the matters of the underworld. My strength cannot sustain it. He was thus able to foresee impending calamities and misfortunes.

He immediately prepared for it, yet he never spoke of it openly for six years. Later, when his mother passed away, he recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and no longer acted as an official for the underworld.
He spoke extensively of the power of this merit, urging his descendants to chant and recite it. Subsequently, he served as the Governor of Qingzhou.
At the age of eighty-four, as he was about to die, he suddenly smelled a wondrous fragrance unlike anything found in this world. He said... [left incomplete].
The man on the right said, "A sage has come to meet me and is heading toward the West. Having finished speaking, he vanished (from the *Baoying ji*).

Pei Xuanli of the Tang dynasty served as Minister of the Ministry of Land during the reign of Empress Wu. He regularly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and was once imprisoned for an offense.
Xie Xu was distressed by his impending execution; he did nothing but recite the sutra with utmost sincerity. One day, his shackles fell off of their own accord.

The investigating magistrate visited him personally and subsequently granted him a pardon. Ren Zhi, who had been imprisoned alongside him, also recited the sutra and was likewise released (from the *Baoying ji*).

Wu Sixuan of the Tang dynasty served as a University Doctor during the reign of Empress Wu. He was a devotee of Śākyamuni and maintained the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, reciting it twice daily.
He experienced many miraculous responses. Later, he grew somewhat lax and recited it only once per day. While Sixuan was ill in the capital, there was a sorcerer...
Chu Xi’er was one whose words regarding matters were like those of a deity. When Xingxia offered prayers, Sīxuán went to visit Xi’er, who said in astonishment, "What arts do you possess?
Ghosts see you and all flee. Sīxuán privately realized this was due to the power of the scriptures and redoubled his diligent cultivation.
He recited it five times daily. His son fell ill, and the physicians were ineffective. Sīxuán recited the scripture with a sincere heart; after three days, the boy recovered.
Once, at the Wei Bridge, Sīxuán saw an old man over eighty years of age wearing coarse mourning clothes. He asked him:
She was the mother who gave birth to me. He pondered this as a mysterious marvel. She replied: "When I was forty-three years old, a strange monk instructed me, saying:
'Do you wish for long life? Simply recite the Diamond Sūtra. My mother immediately resolved her mind to recite it twice daily until she reached the age of one hundred and seven.
Her maternal aunt and a neighbor woman also recited it, and both lived past the age of one hundred. Now I follow my mother’s practice; it has already been nine [years]."
Ten [cases] (from the *Baoying ji*; the characters following "Zun" contain errors). At Yinshan in Raozhou, there was an elder;
his mining households numbered over ten thousand, all of whom lived in thatched huts. During the Yanhe era, a fire broke out, and all ten thousand dwellings were [consumed].
Everything was consumed by fire, yet only the house of one family remained untouched. At that time, Yang Tiji of the local commandery personally questioned the old man.
The old man replied, "My family serves the Buddha and upholds the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. (Recorded in the *Baoying ji*).

Cui Wenjian of the Tang dynasty served as the Sima (Vice Governor) of Fangzhou during the Xuantian era. When the Tibetan forces suddenly descended upon the prefectural city, he was captured along with others and placed under extremely strict shackles and fetters.
He recited the sutras with single-minded devotion; after three days, his shackles suddenly opened of their own accord. The raiders suspected that there was something supernatural about him.

The official interrogated him with the use of the whip and staff, and he answered truthfully. When asked, "What skill do you possess? he replied, "I recite the Diamond Sūtra. He was then ordered to be shackled;
before his recitation was finished, the shackles were removed again. The assembly all marveled at this wonder, and he was subsequently sent out of the jurisdiction (as recorded in the *Baoying ji*).

Yao Daichang (or Yao Daidai) was a native of Zizhou. He constantly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and also commissioned one hundred copies for his mother. Suddenly, a deer appeared and played about him;

seeing people, it was not startled, and even when dogs were present, they did not bark. After lingering for a while, it departed of its own accord. There was once a man slaughtering a sheep who called out to him...
He was told to wait for his meal. As soon as he had finished eating, he died. A messenger led him away and showed him a city gate with an inscription above it;
he was then ushered inside to see the King. The King asked, "How did you come to eat meat? He replied, "Although I ate meat, I have always maintained my recitation of the sutras.

The King praised him, saying, "Since you are able to maintain the recitation of the sutras, why do you not cease eating meat? Thereupon, he was restored to life and wrote out the sutras for his mother. There was a butcher...
The boy Li Huinu requested one scroll [of this scripture] and burned incense to make offerings to it. After Huinu died, someone saw him in the underworld;
his shackles and chains fell away of their own accord, and he was reborn in a good realm (from the *Baoying ji*).
Lu Wen-zhan of the Tang dynasty:
During the third year of the Kaiyuan era, Lu Wen-zhan served as the County Vice Magistrate of Langzhong.

He was deeply devoted to Buddhist scriptures and especially dedicated himself to the recitation of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, reaching more than thirty thousand recitations. His spiritual responses were marvelous and extraordinary. As he grew old and his years declined, three [wisdom] teeth...
His teeth fell out as well. He recited sutras and made earnest supplications, and his teeth grew back as they were before. While he was in Langzhong, there was a severe drought;

the Prefect Liu Jun ordered him to pray for rain, and after only one round of prayers, it poured down copiously. Later, during a period of heavy rains and flooding, the Vice-Governor sent him to pray for clear weather, and it became sunny immediately.
There were many such instances of verification throughout his life that cannot be cited in full (from the *Baoying ji*).
A death-row prisoner in Chang’an County:
After being incarcerated for more than forty days, a death-row prisoner in Chang’an County recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* without ceasing.

As he was about to be executed, his shackles fell away; light emanated from his head, extending for several tens of zhang and illuminating the entire county. The Magistrate reported this to the throne.
Emperor Xuanzong subsequently pardoned his crime (as recorded in the *Guang yiji*).
In the fifteenth year of the Kaiyuan era of the Tang dynasty, Emperor Li Xu issued an edict that all small Buddhist halls throughout the villages of the empire were to be demolished. The work...

The relics were moved to a nearby Buddhist temple. All large halls were ordered to be sealed off. Heretics throughout the empire, upon hearing the news, began tearing them down at the mere sight of it;

even great buildings and colossal statues were destroyed. When the imperial decree reached Yuzhou, Li Xu, the Magistrate of Xinxi, was a man who indulged in wine and was stubborn and headstrong, acting in a contrary and perverse manner.
He was in the midst of a drunken stupor when the provincial edict arrived, which set a three-day deadline.

The Daily Report states: Xujian was greatly incensed and immediately issued a decree that anyone within his jurisdiction who demolished [the temple] would be put to death. Consequently, the entire precinct was preserved intact.

Xujian was a man who delighted in killing, was obstinate and cruel, and whose actions invariably contravened the Way. At that time, it was not out of any regard for the Buddhist monastery that he acted thus.

He preserved his integrity solely because of his resentment and indignation, yet he did not dwell upon this preservation even in his mind. After more than a year, he suffered from a chronic illness for several days.

He died during the height of summer; the body was encoffined the very night before, and the funeral was to take place the following day. As the mother and son circumambulated the coffin weeping, [the account continues].

After a long night, the weeping ceased. From within the coffin, there was heard a sound like fingernails or claws scraping against the wood; at first, they suspected it was a rat, but did not realize its true nature.

In a short while, the sound grew more intense. His wife and children fled in alarm, but his mother alone did not leave. She ordered the coffin opened. His attendants said, "It is the height of summer; we fear it will rot.
The mother, however, grew angry and urged them to open it. Inside lay a hollow shell; the body was quite mangled and festering. Thereupon, she bathed it and intended to...
He nursed him, and after more than a month, he had recovered. Xu said: "At first, I was detained by two soldiers and brought before the King, but the King was not present.
I saw an official at the foot of the steps; it was the magistrate of Xinxi, whom I had not seen for years. Seeing me, he bowed and asked, 'How have you, my superior, managed to come here?
Xu replied, 'I have just been summoned and arrived. The official said, 'Throughout your life, my superior, you did nothing but kill.'"

"You are a man of heart, yet you were unaware of your transgressions and merits; now you must undergo retribution—what will you do? You have heard this in vain and are filled with fear; we pray that you will save us.
The official said, "Last year, when the Buddha hall was demolished, this official’s jurisdiction alone remained intact;
such merit is truly vast. Although the official is dead, it is not appropriate for him to be summoned here. In a moment, the King will question you; say no more, but simply [speak] thus..."
"Yes," Xu replied, and he recalled it after a moment. Soon, King Wuzhuo had Xu led before him. The King said, "Bring forth the ledger of good and evil deeds for Magistrate Li Mingfu.
Immediately, someone brought a large case file, as thick as a man’s embrace, followed by two youths dressed in green.
The King ordered the register opened and the offenses proclaimed. A court official read aloud: "He was particularly fond of cutting off sheep's hooves."
The official said, "He should receive one hundred lashes and have one hundred jin of his own flesh cut off. The King said, "Let him have his flesh cut off.
Xu said, "Last year there was an imperial decree to dismantle Buddhist halls and destroy Buddha images; within my jurisdiction alone, these were preserved. May this merit suffice to offset my crimes?
The King asked in surprise, "Is this truly so? The official replied, "It is not. A new official from Xixi stepped forward and said:
"There is a register of merit in heaven; you may consult it. The King said, "Consult it at once. To the south of the palace wall, there were several rooms on a tower.
An official ascended the tower to consult it, but before he had arrived, two monks came before the palace.

The King asked, "What do you masters possess? One replied, "I constantly recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. The other said, "I constantly read the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. The King rose and joined his palms in reverence.
He said, "Please ask the Dharma Master to ascend the steps. Behind the royal throne were two high seats: one of gold on the right and one of silver on the left.
The King requested that the reciter sit upon the golden seat and the reader sit upon the silver seat. Once they were seated, the scripture was opened, and the King joined his palms to listen.
As the recitation and reading were nearing completion, suddenly five-colored clouds appeared before the golden seat, and purple clouds arrived before the silver seat, where the two monks sat.
They ascended on clouds and flew away, vanishing into the air. The King said to those below the steps, "Did you see the two monks? They have both been reborn in heaven.

Thereupon, the officials examined the registers of merit, and there was but a single sheet remaining. Reading it, they said: "Last year, when the imperial decree ordered the demolition of Buddhist halls, the entire county of Xinxi alone remained intact.
This shall cancel the sins of one lifetime and extend his life by thirty years; he shall furthermore be reborn in a realm of goodness."
"Way! As he finished speaking, fire erupted from within the scrolls of the Register of Sins and consumed them entirely. The King said, "Release Magistrate Li Mingfu and allow him to return.
He then commanded two officials to escort him out through the southern city gate. There, he saw men and women sitting together along both sides of the road in tall pavilions and large houses;

they were drinking and singing to the accompaniment of flutes and songs, their appreciation for music being superficial. Seeing this, he was delighted by it. The two officials said to him, "Pass quickly past this."

Xu did not look back, for he thought that looking back would surely cause harm. He saw the drinking place from afar, but his mind could not bear to go there; he stood still and watched it. A person inside the shop called out, "Come!
Xu said, "This is no good place. Since you do not trust me, you may leave as you please.

Xu had not yet realized the situation. When he arrived at the drinking place, everyone rose; they took their seats and music was played on stringed and wind instruments. Once the wine was served, Xu finished the ritual of mutual salutations and toasts. Just as he was about to...
He was told to drink it; it was a cup of excrement, foul and loathsome beyond measure.
Xu refused to drink it, whereupon a bull-headed hell-warden emerged from beneath the bed and pierced his chest through with a fork. Startled, Xu hurriedly drank several cups and then departed.
The officers led Xu Nan into a narrow path through a desolate field. From afar, they saw a lamp burning brightly; beside the lamp was a great pit, pitch black and bottomless.
The two officers pushed him into it, whereupon he revived. Li Xu was by nature fierce and stubborn, ignorant of sin and merit.
Having been intoxicated, he acted in defiance, claiming that the restoration of the Buddha hall was not his original intention. Nevertheless—
It was as if his very body had been reborn in heaven; the fire consumed his register of sins, and the blessings he obtained were such as these. Is this not the retribution for doing good?

As for those who exert themselves with diligence day and night, laboring earnestly to do good—upholding the monastic discipline and constantly practicing the Buddha’s words—it has never happened that they did not transcend birth and death (from *Jiwen*).

During the Kaiyuan era of the Tang dynasty, there was a member of the Lu clan who resided in Huazhou. One day, while sitting idly in the main hall during the daytime, he saw two men dressed in yellow tunics enter the door.
The Lu man asked, "Who are you? They replied, "We are the village headmen (lizheng). We have come with an official warrant to summon you. The Lu man was greatly... [frightened].

He was startled and asked why he was being pursued. When the man explained that he had been sent to fetch him so he might view the inscription, he saw that the seal was marked with the characters for "Wei County.

Upon opening it, he found the characters were erroneous and did not resemble the handwriting of a human being. Finding this strange, he interrogated the official. The official replied, "I have received orders to pursue you; I do not know the reason.
Suddenly, he saw a horse already prepared at the foot of the steps. Having no choice, he mounted the horse and departed, looking back at [the official].
A corpse sat upon the bed; his heart felt profound revulsion. In the midst of such urgency, he did not realize it was dead.
Furthermore, he saw horses emerging, not through the gates, but all walking along the walls. He was then struck with terror and wept aloud, only then realizing that death was certain.

He regretted not having been able to bid farewell to his mother and sisters before traveling some tens of li. Upon reaching a city, he found it to be exceedingly magnificent. He asked, "What is this place?"

The city was that of a kingdom, as the official stated. He immediately sent word to his own authorities. After entering the city, the official wished to present Lu to the king. As they passed through a courtyard, he asked, "What courtyard is this?
The official replied, "This is the courtyard of the Minister of Justice (Yushi Dafu). Lu then inquired, "What are the name and surname of the Minister of Justice?

The official said, "His surname is Li and his given name is So-and-so. Lu was filled with joy and surprise, and said to the official, "This is my cousin. The official then ordered [him to be introduced].
The official delivered his visiting card. In a short while, he came out; they met with great joy and spoke at length of their past acquaintance. He invited him in to sit and converse.
The Grand Master said, "Your younger brother’s merit from recitation is truly vast.

This is entirely due to the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, which is the very marrow and bone of the holy teachings, and possesses profound, inconceivable merit. When Lu first entered the monastery, he saw several dozen...
The people were all dressed in official robes and caps. Later, more than half of them were found ensnared in nets; some were without clothes, and others had their heads bared.
Lu asked, "Who are all these people? They replied, "These are officials from the land of Yangdi. Those within the nets are all here because their sins are heavy.
If you, younger brother, could preach the Dharma for them once, all who see it would ascend to heaven. He then ordered a high seat to be brought and had Lu ascend and sit upon it.
As they recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, those within the net began to lift their heads;

by the midpoint of the recitation, they had all emerged upon the ground—some wearing wide-sleeved robes and others riding in carriages or driving through the clouds. When the recitation was finished, everyone had been reborn.
Upon entering to have an audience with the King, he addressed them as "Dharma Masters" and paid them profound respect. The King said, "You have done a great thing..."
It was inconceivable; even calculation could not exhaust it. He marveled at the power of recitation and immediately ordered the official to send him back.

Upon arriving home, he saw his family with disheveled hair, weeping, while his corpse lay upon the ground. His heart was deeply moved by compassion. Suddenly, a maidservant entered the hall from the courtyard;
the official ordered her to ascend the steps, and as she stepped forward, the spirit suddenly re-entered the body. Thereupon—
This man subsequently recovered his life (from the *Guang yiji*).
Chen Libin was a native of Kuaiji.
Having attained the rank of *mingjing* at the age of twenty, he excelled in composing prose and poetry. Upon receiving his official robes, he served as a *Chang...* (the text is incomplete).
The City Commandant, Bing, had recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* since his youth. Whenever he encountered misfortune or hardship, he frequently received its protection.
During the Kaiyuan era, Bing traveled from Kuaiji in Jiangzhou to Dongyang. It happened that there had been heavy rain for many days, and the river waters were overflowing.

Bing set out with more than twenty other vessels carrying his followers; they hoisted their sails to catch the wind, but in a mere moment the sky grew dark and the force of the wind intensified. Upon reaching...
Above a stone grotto in the river, a dam obstructed the flow of the waters so that waves crashed against it with such force that they could not settle.

More than twenty vessels from the preceding generation had all reached the mouth of this grotto and been wrecked. The boatmen were terrified; however, Lìbīn hurriedly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
When he reached the rushing current, a creature resembling a red dragon suddenly emerged across the stream, supporting the boat so that it was able to pass through.
[End of] the upper section. Commentators say this is due to the merit of reciting the sutras (*Guang yiji*).
Wang Hong:
Wang Hong was a man who, in his youth, made his living by fishing and hunting. During the Tianbao era of the Tang dynasty, he once released a hawk to pursue a rabbit and ran off.
Xuēhóng followed and explored it, where he found one fascicle of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
From that time on, he no longer hunted (from the *Guǎng yì jì*). — Tánshì.
Tian, the District Magistrate of Yizhou, was by nature fond of hunting; he constantly kept falcons and hounds as his primary occupation.

At the beginning of the Tianbao era of the Tang dynasty, while releasing a falcon in the thickets and brambles of Yizhou, he discovered a scroll of scripture. Upon taking it up and examining it, he found it to be the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
From that time forth, he resolved to practice it; after several years of recitation, he had already completed more than two thousand repetitions. Nevertheless, he did not cease his hunting.

He ceased [his practice]. Later, he encountered an illness and died suddenly. After several days, he was summoned and arrived at the Underworld. He saw various birds and beasts surrounding an area of several mu, which were demanding his life.
Shortly thereafter, he followed them there and saw the King. The King asked, "Why are your offenses so numerous? Tian was unable to answer.
The King ordered his officials to take them away for interrogation. When the ten men reached the magistrate’s office, the official ordered them to open their mouths;

he threw a single pill into each mouth, whereupon it immediately burst into flames. In an instant, their entire bodies were reduced to ashes, but shortly thereafter they were restored to human form once more.
In this manner, six or seven individuals reached the field of Mr. Tian (Tiánshì). Although he stacked three pellets [of fire-starting material], no sign of fire appeared.
The officials found this strange and brought him before the King to report the facts in detail. The King asked, "What meritorious deeds did you perform while alive?
Mr. Tian replied, "In my youth, I made my living by hunting. The King questioned him further, saying, "While you were alive, you obtained gold from atop a thorn tree in Yizhou."
She had already recited the *Diamond Sūtra* more than two thousand times. The King said, "This very act shall extinguish all her sins.

He ordered his attendants to check the register of merits for the Tian family, and they returned with a report exactly as he had said. The King then personally instructed the lady Tian to recite the sūtra;

after only three pages, she looked back into the courtyard and saw that neither the birds nor the beasts were there anymore. When the recitation was finished, the King praised her, saying, "To have recited it two thousand times!"
His life span was extended by fifteen years, and he was subsequently permitted to return home (*from the Guǎng yì jì*).
*Tàipíng guǎngjì*, Section on Retribution (Part 1);
*Tàipíng guǎngjì*, Section on Retribution (Part 2).
Li Weiyen was the Magistrate of Jiande County. In his youth, he had maintained the practice of reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

Toward the end of the Tianbao era of the Tang dynasty, while serving as a subordinate officer (*canjun*) in Yuyao Commandery, Li Weiyen was returning north upon the completion of his term. As he passed through Wuzhang Village, the embankment dam at Shangyu Jiang broke, and the waters surged forth.
At the time of midnight, when it was dark and gloomy and no one was within four paces, this road had long been frequented by bandits.
There were several hundred bolts of Wu silk in Yan’s boat; fearing they would be seized by thieves, he took up a sword and went before the boat to recite sutras.
After the third watch, he saw two torches on the embankment approaching from afar. Only Yan suspected they were villagers protecting him;
when the fires reached a hundred paces from the boat, they suddenly turned back. He found this quite extraordinary and redoubled his efforts, chanting the sutras with an even more forceful voice.

I also reflected privately to myself: "Could this not be due to the power of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*? At that time, the water in the pond had dried up, yet the water outside the pond was full.
Only Yan Bian thought to himself, "If the pond breaks, I shall surely receive the aid of the water. After half the night had passed, [the pond broke].

Suddenly, he heard the sound of flowing water at the bow of the boat. Startled, he exclaimed, "The embankment is several zhang wide; how could it have been breached? After a long while, he gradually felt the boat rising.
By dawn, the river water had already filled the vessel. Facing the boat, there was a hole several feet wide, whereupon he realized the truth.
Regarding the assistance provided by reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*: it is said that Wei Yan and his younger brother Wei Yu were serving as Vice Governors of Qianzhou.

Seeing that their elder brother had achieved merit through the recitation of the sutra, they followed his example. Later, while traveling by boat out of the Gorges, the current was swift and the oar broke;

the boat was on the verge of capsizing, so they recited the sutra with all their might. Suddenly, they saw an oar being carried down by the flow, which they then recovered. Their kinsmen were likewise saved.
He constantly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. During the rebellion of An Lushan, he lay hidden in the wild grass.
As the rebels drew near, he thought of obtaining a single shoe to flee. Suddenly, something fell upon his back; looking up in alarm, it was a new pair of shoes (from the *Guang yi ji*).
Sun Ming-tang:
Sun Ming was a native of Yangwu in Zhengzhou. His family had been poor and lowly for generations, and he served as a tenant farmer on the estate of the Lu clan.

He was skilled at reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, chanting it twenty times every day. This continued for twenty years; from the very beginning of his practice, he had abstained from meat and pungent roots.
Later, while he was reciting with right mindfulness, two officials suddenly appeared to pursue him. Mingyi, thinking they were county officials, went toward them.
After traveling about five or six li, he arrived at the gate of a palace. The gatekeeper said, "The King has already gone out. Consequently, the patrol official confined Mingyi in an empty room.
That room extended for fifty or sixty bays in width and length, its roof like a mass of overhanging clouds. Seven days passed.
Just as the King was arriving, the official led Ming into the palace. The King asked, "What merit do you possess? He replied, "I have upheld the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* for twenty years.
The King said, "This is a great merit. Turning to his attendants, he said, "Yesterday I received a report from the Jetavana monastery stating that Ming’s recitation has been diligent and earnest;
I request that his term be extended by twenty years. Thus it was known that the cultivation of the Way is inconceivable.
He was detained for twenty years to compensate for his service. An official was ordered to escort him back to his home.

Although the family had already completed the enshrinement of Ming’s remains, they were unaware that the spirit had returned to his body. It happened that a hunter passed by the tomb chamber and heard the sound of crying;
he informed Ming’s family, and thus he was restored to life. By the end of the Tianbao era, Ming had been alive for six or seven years.
"I am quite well" (from the *Guang yiji*).
Regarding the "Three Sword Masters" of the Tang dynasty: their secular surname was Zhang, and their given name was Boying. During the Qiannian era, he served as a soldier in Shouzhou. By nature...
He was a man of supreme filial piety. Because his father was in Yingzhou, he stole an official horse to go and welcome him for a visit. Upon reaching Huaiyin, he was captured by the city guards.
The Prefect, Cui Zhao, ordered that he be executed by decapitation outside the city walls. At that time, the executioner was renowned for his skill with the blade;

yet when he struck twice, the victim’s body remained entirely unhurt. The executioner then changed to a sharper blade and hacked with all his might, but it remained as undamaged as before. The executioner...
Startled, he said, "When I used my knife to strike his body, my hand became limp; I do not know why. He immediately reported this to Zhao, who asked for the reason.
He replied, "In my fifteenth year, I once abstained from meat and blood, and I have recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* for over ten years."

Since the onset of the Hu rebellion, he had remained within the military and no longer engaged in recitation. Yesterday, having been subjected to an unforeseen punishment, his resolve was such that he focused solely on reciting the sutras.

Zhaō sighed and let him go; thereupon, he shaved his head and left the household life. He wore large iron bells and went begging for alms, performing a vegetarian feast for a thousand people which he prepared in a single day.
People of the time called him the "Three-Swords Master," saying he was one who [could rise from the dead].
*Jing pusa* (from the *Guang yi ji*).
Song Canjun of Fangzhou:

Song Canjun of Fangzhou had maintained the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* since his youth. When he was appointed as an official and took up temporary residence at the residence of the Director of the Office of Personnel (*Sishu*), he stayed there.
Sengjue was aware that his residence was ill-omened; every evening he would invariably recite the sutras. Suddenly, he saw a woman standing outside his door.
After a long while, Sengjue asked, "Are you not a ghost? She replied, "Indeed. He asked again, "The realms of the unseen and the seen differ in principle;

it is not fitting for us to meet. Is there some grievance or injustice concerning you? The woman then wept bitterly and said, "It is so. I am the wife of the former Director of the Office of Personnel (Sishi)."
The Director of Personnel was on an official mission. His younger brother, being coerced by him, refused to comply and was consequently killed.
The corpse was wrapped in felt and thrown into a latrine in the northwest corner of the hall. The accumulation of filth became unbearable, and many people came wishing to lodge a complaint;

yet, as laypeople are timid and fearful upon seeing the sight, their grievances remained suppressed and the perpetrator’s cruelty did not come to light. Suddenly, we hear that you, sir, have taken charge of the matter.
"Reciting [the scriptures] shall be your merit; you should also extensively protect all sentient beings. Seeing that you have been defiled by such impurity, how could I not pity you?
Song Yun said, "At present my official rank is low, so I cannot save you alone. Tomorrow I will certainly report this to the Magistrate, and then the ghost will depart.
When morning came, he reported this in full detail. They dug the earth and searched the latrine, but did not find her corpse. As Song Yun recited the sutras, the woman appeared once more.
Question: Why was it not obtained? Answer: It is said, "It is only one chi away to the northwest; you should seek it tomorrow to fulfill my kindness.
Following these words, he indeed obtained it; within the felt mat, only the bones remained. He washed them again and moved them to another location.
That evening, he came again to offer his thanks. With great joy, he said, "Your protection has been so profound that it is difficult to repay.
Although I am in the realm of the unseen, there is still communication to be had. You have two sons; the elder will be difficult to sustain, but the younger will surely attain success.

Later, he shall hold a position of honor. He further spoke of the successive changes in official rank and emolument during the Song dynasty, adding, "I am deeply ashamed that you, Excellency, were unaware of this."
"How can I repay you? she asked. When Song saw the Prefect, he related their discussion in detail. The Prefect then asked what office she held herself.
That evening, the woman arrived again and conveyed the Prefect’s message, saying that her appointment would be changed within one month, though it would not be to her satisfaction.
When he was about to be transferred to the position of Vice Governor of Guizhou, Song Ji reported these matters to him, and all were found to be verified.
Initially, when Song Ji asked, "Since my body has already been killed by someone, why do you not take revenge? [the deity] replied, "The person before me is currently still serving as an official;
his life span has not yet reached its end, which is why I have not yet retaliated. (From the *Guang yiji*).
Liu Hongjian was a descendant of Liu Zhan, a former Grand Minister of the Censorate. At the beginning of the Qianyuan era of the Tang dynasty, he fled south during the chaos.
A monk instructed him to recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, and Hongjian recited it daily. By the first year of the Shangyuan era, he was lodging in Shouchun.
One day, as he was leaving his gate, he suddenly saw two officials who said, "We have received a warrant from the Grand Marshal ordering us to arrest Hongjian.

He replied, "I do not even know the Grand Marshal; why do you command me? Intending to resist, he was suddenly seized by the two officials, who dragged him forward and demanded that he put on his robe.
The officials refused to let go and continued to pull him along. Before long, they had suddenly crossed the Huai River and arrived at a village. In a brief moment—
He took a hempen robe and a waist-belt and had Hongjian put them on. Laughing, he said, "This is truly a great 'sour' robe. Thereupon, they traveled northward;
the road gradually became more difficult and obstructed. Upon reaching a large city, they entered it and found a government office that was extremely solemn and magnificent.
Suddenly, the monk who had previously encouraged him to recite the sutras emerged from the official residence. A youth following behind the monk recognized Hongjian and went straight toward him.
The person asked, "Sixteenth Young Master, why have you come here? He then ran to inform the monk, saying, "Liu Sixteenth was just now pursued by an official.
Since he has recited the sutras, how could you not go there to save him? Hongjian soon arrived at the monk's quarters and prostrated himself reverently to beg for help.
The monk said, "My disciple shall suffer no hardship. In a short while, the official led Hongjian inside.
Behind the desk in the hall, there was a five-colored stupa, three or four feet high, which was spinning and turning.
Before he could question it, the monk had already entered the gate; the stupa transformed into a handsome man about thirty years of age, who said, "I am the Minister of the Interior."
Descending the steps, he received the monk’s question: "Why has the Master returned? The monk replied, "Liu Hongjian is your own disciple.
His cultivation of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* has reached such a high degree that his allotted lifespan is not yet exhausted; it is fitting that he be seen by you.
The King said, "If he has been reciting the *Vajracchedikā*, I wish to hear it. He then ordered him to kneel and recite. After Hongjian had finished reciting two pages, suddenly—
In the Hall of Oblivion, there was a man to the west holding a golden hook and a dragon-headed banner. On the banner were green characters inscribing the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
He spread it before Hongjian and commanded him to recite the sutra clearly. When he had finished, the person vanished entirely, leaving only the hall and its buildings behind.
It became silent and still. Upon leaving the gate, he saw only pursuing officials. Suddenly, there was a form resembling two suns that came to strike Hongjian.
Terrified, Hongjian fled; suddenly he saw water by the side of the road, and Hongjian wished to stop and drink from it.
The pursuing officer said, "This is human fat; it has merely been clear for a long time. Beneath it is all nothing but leftover skin and putrid flesh. Once you have drunk this, there is no returning.
In a short while, they arrived at the house and saw the skeletal form lying upon the bed. His heart was filled with profound sorrow.
The ghost pushed him from behind, and he entered the room as if in a state of deep slumber; he then revived. Having obtained the money, the ghost departed.
(From the *Guang yiji*).
Zhang Jiayou of Guangling was serving as the Sima of Mingzhou at the beginning of the Baoying era of the Tang dynasty when he fell ill and died. His coffin was then carried back...

He returned home and was buried outside the South Gate of Guangling. At the beginning of the Yongtai era, one of his former acquaintances, a man surnamed Lao, was traveling south of the city wall when he sat down beneath a stupa.
Suddenly, he saw Huizhou riding a white horse approaching from the south. Upon seeing Lao, Huizhou dismounted;
they comforted one another as they had in life, yet Huizhou did not remove his ceremonial cap and spoke with his head bowed. Lao asked him about the world of the dead.
"What are sins and blessings? Yu replied, "Sins and blessings are manifest; there is nothing that is not obtained in accordance with what one does.

However, I have long upheld the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, and now I have attained freedom from karmic entanglement. I shall also surely find another destination within a matter of ten days or a month.
When you return, tell my elder brother to recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* one thousand times for me. Why did you take my incense burner?"
“Those evil things! Your family also possesses two fascicles of scripture; I would be grateful if you would recite them for me to increase my own merit.
Having said this, he took his leave and departed. [The narrator] was so exhausted and dazed that it was a long time before he regained consciousness (from the *Guang yi ji*).

Wei Xun of the Tang dynasty was the son of Shangde, the Left Attendant-in-Ordinary. He upheld the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. At the beginning of the Shengong era, he served as a General of the Gate Guard (*Jianmenwei Da Jiangjun*).
At that time, there was a man in the capital named Cai Ce who died suddenly; after several days, he revived and said: "When I first arrived..."

In the underworld, the officials were frustrated because they could not capture the man. They were about to flog their messengers when the messengers reported, "General Wei Xun holds the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*;
benevolent deities protect him, so we cannot capture him. Thereupon, other messengers were dispatched to pursue him again, but upon their return shortly thereafter, the report was identical.
The infernal official said, "Cease the pursuit for now. When Wei Xun heard this, he redoubled his diligent practice (from the *Guang yi ji*).

Du Sine was a native of Tongqi County in Lu Prefecture during the Tang dynasty. Du Sine recovered from a serious illness through the power of his recitation of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
On every day he recited the sutra, he would invariably behold a divine radiance (as recorded in the *Guang yi ji*).

The Abbot of Longxing Monastery [was from] Tang Yuanzhou. On account of a great vegetarian assembly, the abbot gathered the monks; as his years of ordination (*śrāmaṇera-varṣa*) were already advanced, he was a man of long-standing virtue.
He sat beneath the seat of the distinguished guest, Piṇḍola-bharadvāja. A young monk arrived later from outside, having no place to sit.
Only one seat remained vacant for the temple master at the lower end of the row. As the junior monk was about to sit, the temple master suddenly rebuked him. This occurred several times.

Fearing that the meal would be missed, the junior monk finally came forward and took his seat. The temple master became exceedingly enraged; leaning against a pillar, he reached out with his palm to strike him.

Just as he was about to bring his hand down, his large sleeves were caught and pressed by the pillar so that they could not be lowered. With palms joined in alarm, the junior monk was struck with terror.

The monk was ashamed and discouraged; without partaking in the meal, he returned to his room. The assembly discussed the matter, fearing it might be due to the spiritual power (*moral virtue*) of this young monk.
The temple master, together with the monastic community, went to pay their respects to the young monk. Terrified, he declared, "I have never practiced the Way in my life;

I did not dare to indiscriminately receive the honors due to one of Great Virtue. He hesitated for a moment and then fled. Thereupon, they asked him what kind of religious practice he had performed throughout his life. He replied, "Two..."
For ten years, he had maintained only the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Everyone marveled at this, attributing it to the power of the Vajra’s protection.
He then burned incense and prostrated before the pillar, reciting a mantra: "If this is indeed the spiritual power of the Vajra, let this garment be returned.
Thereupon, it emerged from the pillar as soon as his hand reached for it (from the *Guang yiji*).
Chen Zhe of Lin’an:
Chen Zhe was a native of Yuhang. He was single-minded in his cultivation and practiced ascetic discipline. He recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāra-mitā Sūtra*.
At the beginning of the Guangde era, the bandit Song Tan from Wukang raided Yuhang. Chen Zhe, who possessed great wealth, intended to move his property to avoid the danger.
Before long, the bandits arrived. Daozhe took them for government troops and asked how far away they were.
The bandits were furious and cried out, "What kind of old dog dares to insult us? They vied with one another to stab him with their swords.

Yet, with every stroke of a sword, a five-colored circular light, five or six feet in diameter, would shield Daozhe’s body so that they could not pierce him. The bandits were struck with awe and marveled, saying he must be a sage.
There was no one who did not feel shame and remorse; they abandoned [the object] and departed (from the *Guang yiji*).
Zhang Yi, a watchtower guard at Fengzhou (both of the above two accounts are recorded in the *Jiuyi*).
Zhang Guoying.

During the early Dali era of the Tang dynasty, when Cui Ning was stationed in Western Shu, the rebellion of Yang Lin broke out. A soldier named Zhang Guoying engaged him in battle and struck him in the abdomen with an arrow;

He wept as he bid farewell to his fellow soldiers. Guo Ying habitually recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. One night, he dreamed that a foreign monk gave him a pill.
At dawn, he discharged an arrowhead, and the wound immediately closed and healed (from the *Baoying ji*).
Wang Xiaolian (in *Zai Jiuyi*):
Li Tingguang of the Tang dynasty served as the Commandant of Dezhou. He revered the Buddha and abstained from meat and blood, constantly upholding the *Vajra[-sūtra]*.
Whenever he recited the sutras, a circular halo would appear before him. If his mental application reached a state of extreme intensity, the light gradually grew larger;

if he harbored even a slight trace of indolence, the light gradually diminished and grew dim. Because of this, he sharpened his resolve and redoubled his diligent progress (as recorded in the *Baoying ji*).
Lu Kangcheng of the Tang dynasty once served as a legal clerk (facao chuan) in the capital of Jingzhao Prefecture. He did not shrink from confronting the powerful or the oppressive.

Once, after retiring from official duties, he suddenly saw a deceased subordinate carrying several hundred sheets of documents and requesting his signature. Lu asked, "Since you have already passed away, how could you come here? The man replied: [The remainder of the text follows the narrative of the deceased official.]
Kang Cheng looked at these registers of the netherworld office; they contained only the names of people and lacked almost any other information.

The official said, "These are all those who will die by the blade next year. Kang Cheng asked, "Is there not one among them that is me? If so, please check and show it to me. The official replied, "There is."

He was greatly alarmed and said, "Since you were formerly my official, could you not have some feeling for me? He replied, "That is precisely why I have come to inform the Honorable Lord. Only the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* can be entrusted; otherwise, I shall lose my life. Thereupon, he proceeded to recite the *Vajracchedikā*, several dozen times each day. The following year, Zhu Ci indeed rebelled. He appointed Kang Cheng as a Censor, but Kang Cheng rebuked him, saying, "A rebel minister dares to interfere with a man of national caliber! Zhu Ci then had him executed. His body was exposed in the marketplace, yet his countenance remained serene and his expression unchanged. When his disciples went to collect his remains, they found that his tongue alone had not decayed. It was over one foot long and three inches thick. They enshrined it in a stupa at the temple of Huayan. Later, during the reign of Emperor Dezong, the monk Huilun of the Great Xingshan Monastery in Chang'an dreamed of a person who told him, "I am the former Censor Kang Cheng. I have been reborn in the Western Paradise. I wish to repay the kindness of my former teacher by bestowing upon you this tongue. The next morning, Huilun went to the temple and saw the tongue displayed there. He took it and enshrined it within a stupa at the monastery. Li Ci was struck with rage and ordered several hundred cavalrymen to surround and shoot at him. Kang Cheng silently recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, yet not a single arrow caused him harm.
Li Ci said, "It is true that for a Confucian, loyalty and integrity serve as armor. He then abandoned his pursuit and departed.
Kang Cheng subsequently retired to live in seclusion on Mount Zhongnan, never again taking office (from the *Baoying ji*).

Xue Yan of Tang was the Sima of Zhongzhou. He maintained a vegetarian diet and observed lifelong fasting, reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* thirty times every day until he reached seventy-two.
As his end approached, he saw banners, canopies, and musical instruments coming to welcome him. His wife, Lady Cui, was the daughter of An [the Grand Master of Remonstrance].
Yan’s paternal aunt was on her deathbed when she saw Yan; she followed behind his ceremonial banners and parasols as he ascended slowly toward heaven.
Though called back, she did not look back, and the entire family smelled the fragrance of a supernatural incense (from the *Baoying ji*).
Ren Zixin (Ren Zixin), a native of Jiazhou, traveled to Hunan during the fifteenth year of the Zhenyuan era of the Tang dynasty.

He habitually recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāraṇī*, which remained pure and white without a single blemish. While on Lake Dongting, a strange object resembling clouds emerged, enveloping his boat; in an instant—
The boat dispersed, and those on board lost their confidence, not knowing where they were. After a long time, they emerged upon the waves and said:

"We have reached the Dragon Palace to pay our respects to the Dragon King. Four or five people were ordered to ascend the hall to recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, after which we were given several dozen precious gems and jewels.
Two monks escorted us out of the palace; one monk entrusted a small amount of these gifts to a believer, who carried them to Mount Heng at the Guanyin Terrace."
Master Shaozhen entrusted him with this, saying, "Your preceptor sent this to you; he instructed that you should recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
He then went to Nanyue to visit a monk, where he indeed saw him and was told, "The Preceptor passed away five or six years ago" (from the *Baoying ji*).
Duan Wenchang (included in the *Preface to the Jiuyi*); Liu Yihuai; Sun Xian and Monk Zhideng;
Lady Wang; and the Private Soldier of the Left Regiment (the above five accounts are all included in the *Jiuyi*);
Song Kan.
Song Kǎn was a native of the Jianghuai region. Having passed the examination for the Classics (míngjīng), at the beginning of the Yuánhé era, he arrived at Hégǔ County.
Due to illness, he abandoned his studies and became a clerk at the Salt and Iron Office, receiving two thousand coins per month. He married and settled there, no longer considering other occupations.
After more than a year, a rice convoy passing through the Sānmén Gorges arrived; because the officials could not read characters, they requested Kǎn to accompany them to manage the ledgers.
The letter stated: "A monthly stipend of eight thousand coins is being granted. Wen Kan said to his wife, "For several months now we have not received eight thousand;
if we can obtain it for a single month, it would be an immense benefit. His wife, Lady Yang, was exceptionally virtuous. She urged him not to go, saying, "The boat route at Sanmen is quite perilous.
Should you suffer injury or danger, what could this profit possibly remedy? Kan would not accept her advice and departed anyway. Upon arriving there—
Suddenly, they were struck by a violent storm, and all the ships sank. Only Huan entered the water and managed to grasp a bundle of grain straw.
Drifting gradually toward the shore, he floated out on the straw and was saved, while the other dozens of people were not rescued.
He then embraced the straw and thanked it, saying: "This humble life of mine is granted by you. I vow that whether we live or die, we shall never part. Thereupon...

Carrying a bundle of straw, he traveled several li at a brisk pace until he came upon a place where an elderly woman sold tea. Her thatched cottage consisted of two rooms, and he went there to stay the night.
He explained his situation in detail, and the old woman took pity on him; she prepared a gruel for him. When morning came, she was hanging clothes out to dry in front of the house.
He untied the straw and spread it out in the sun to dry. Among the straw, he found a bamboo tube; upon opening it, he discovered it was the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
He immediately questioned his mother-in-law about it, but she did not know the details. His mother-in-law said, "This was your wife.

Since you arrived, she has been praying with disheveled hair and copying this scripture with such sincerity that she was able to save you. Kǎn wept with gratitude and requested to take the scripture home; his mother-in-law pointed toward a path to the southeast.
He said, "If you simply continue on this path, it is about two hundred li from here; you can reach home the day after tomorrow.
He gave him two *sheng* of rice, and [Hui]kan bowed in thanks before departing. Indeed, in two days he arrived at Heyin. Seeing his wife, he apologized with shame.

Lady Yang asked in surprise, "How did you know? He recounted the entire matter from beginning to end. Lady Yang marveled at this, whereupon Huikan brought out the sutra, and Lady Yang wept as she prostrated herself.

He bowed his head in reverence. Kan asked, "What shall be used as a mark? [The other] replied, "While copying it, the scribe mistakenly wrote the character for 'arhat' (luóhàn) with the radical for 'empty space' (kōng) above and lacking the four strokes.
I have therefore gone to the Venerable Chan at Huguo Temple to request that he add them. The Venerable was elderly and his vision was failing;
he had passed over the point with his brush so heavily that the characters were all dark and blurred. However, for ten days now, he has not known where they are. Let us examine them.
When the results were exactly as she had described, An bowed again with tears in his voice. Every day, his wife burned incense and paid homage to the scriptures in a pure chamber.
She then said to Lady Yang, "The old woman by the riverbank must not be forgotten. She dispatched a messenger with tea and silk for her;
when the messenger arrived, neither the dwelling nor the person could be seen. She questioned the cowherds, who said, "Recently, the waters have risen and there has been no [sign of her]."
At the edge [of the road], he asked, "Is there anyone selling tea? He replied, "There is no one on the road at all; this must be a divine manifestation.
Several years later, Zheng Yin, the State Councilor, served as the Imperial Resident of the Eastern Capital (Luoyang). He summoned Yankan and Yang Yuan to inquire about the origins of these events.
He further ordered that the sutra be brought and bestowed a military rank upon her son, providing him with a monthly stipend of five thousand coins.

Because he sought this sutra, it has been venerated by the Zheng family to this day. Upon witnessing these events, the Provincial Governor of Yuezhou, the Chancellor and Duke of Hongnong, composed this account, titled "The Miraculous Verification of Lady Yang" (from the *Baoying ji*).
Chen Zhao, Wang Zhongwo (recorded in *Jiuyi*), and Wang Cheng. Wang Cheng was a native of Jinzhou;
he was by nature stubborn and vulgar. In the fourth year of the Yuanhe era of the Tang dynasty, his family suffered from an epidemic, and many died.
When he was eighteen or nineteen, he merely managed to escape [the slaughter]. He then began eating dog meat voraciously, and his eyes subsequently went blind.

Not knowing of medical treatment, he prayed only to spirits and deities for several years without receiving any response. Suddenly, a strange monk invited him to a meal and said to him, "In the scriptures of our Master there is the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*;
it can dispel all suffering and its karmic retribution is swift and miraculous. Layman, would you be able to receive it? Baoci declined.

He was foolish. Furthermore, being blind, it was certainly impossible for him to record it. The monks urged him to transcribe it, and he followed their words. He obtained seven fascicles and requested the monks to recite them.

After several days, he dreamed that the aforementioned monk held a knife and gouged out his eyes. Startled, he awoke; immediately he began to see, and after some time his vision became clear throughout.
Within a few months, it was as it had been before. He spent the rest of his life reciting the sutras without ceasing (from the *Baoying ji*).
Li Yuanyi.
In the fifth year of the Yuanhe era of the Tang dynasty, he served as the Sima of Raozhou. He had a daughter living in a separate courtyard who suddenly saw a divine being one night;
she died from shock and terror, yet her complexion remained unchanged. Her husband, Yan Ne, came from Qin to [the scene].
At Canghu, he suddenly and vaguely saw his wife walking upon the water and approaching him. When Nü asked her in astonishment, she wept and said, "I have already died;
I am now a ghost. Startled and struck by this marvel, Nü said, "Nearby, at Yanpu Village, there is Master Yan."

He instructed his disciples, saying, "That man possesses extraordinary arts. Go and petition him earnestly, entreating him to have pity and save me; perhaps I may yet return to life. Later, Nǜ indeed met Master Yán.
He paid his respects and, weeping, confessed everything from the very beginning. At first, Yán was extremely angry, saying, "Your son suffers from a wind-illness;
why has he come to insult you, Nǜ? Nǜ bowed again and wept piteously. After a long while, [Yán] finally consented, saying, "As for the one who killed your lady..."

Arriving the next day, he reported everything in detail. Yuan-yi transcribed the scripture and was ordered to recite it seven times quickly. Thereupon, the woman opened [the door].
She gazed at it for a long time. Then, speaking with shame and apology, she said to her husband, "Beneath a certain pillar of this hall lies the dry bones of General Wang, clutching a short sword.
This is the very sword for his reburial; I ask that you keep it to repay your kindness.

When they excavated it, it was indeed as verified. They subsequently reinterred him and retained the sword. Yuan-yi then transcribed several hundred scrolls of sutras to bestow upon the netherworld. (From the *Baolin Zhuan*)
