There was a great venomous snake; those in the household who saw it were all struck with terror.

Wan Ying became enraged, and one day, carrying a massive club, he waited for it to emerge, struck and killed it, and cooked and roasted its flesh to eat. Consequently, he fell ill; his internal organs suffered excruciating pain, and he passed away.

His heart remained slightly warm, and after seven days he revived, saying: "At first, I saw three or four messengers from the underworld pursuing me away. We traveled through the darkness for ten [li]..."
In another village, he saw a man walking alone, his radiance encircling his body and illuminating for several feet on all sides.

As the man recited a scripture while walking, [Wanye] approached the light and called out his own surname and name, saying, "My surname is Zhao and my given name is [Name]. I constantly recite the Diamond Sutra; you need only not leave me.
The messenger did not dare to advance further. After a long time, [the light] vanished. He eventually reached the man's home, where Wan Ying bowed to him.
Xie said, "Had I not encountered a supreme person, I certainly would not have returned. That man bestowed upon him the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Having memorized it, Xie returned home.
Upon being reborn, he took up the original text and recited it again; there were no further omissions or errors. His illness also vanished.
Consequently, he renounced wine and meat and ceased all killing. He recited the sūtra fifty times every day (from the *Baoying ji*).
Regarding Li Hui:
Li Hui was a candidate for the jinshi examination. In the eighth year of the Yuanhe era of the Tang dynasty, he was unsuccessful in his attempt and was about to return home.

A monk advised him, saying, "If you, young master, wish to attain the degree quickly, why do you not recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*? He subsequently recited it several dozen times daily until he reached Wangqiao Bridge.

While walking under the moon due to past karmic conditions, he encountered a beautiful woman who, upon speaking with him, enticed him away for more than ten *li* until they reached a village dwelling.
There, she laughed and chatted very warmly with him as she led him inside to the hall. He saw five or six people, all of whom were young women.
Li Hui feared they might be malevolent spirits, so he secretly recited a sutra. Suddenly, a strange light issued from his mouth, and the group of women were struck with terror and fled. However—
He smelled a foul and putrid odor; it was evidently the dwelling place of foxes and wildcats, with brambles and thorns filling his sight. Li Hui stood dazed, not knowing where to go.
Suddenly, a white dog appeared, its color whiter than frost or snow, as if leading Li Hui forward.
Light emanated from its mouth, further illuminating the path. After hesitating for a moment, they reached their original destination (from the *Baoying ji*).
Qiang Bodai of Tang.
In the ninth year of the Yuanhe era, he resided in Fangzhou. His family had been afflicted by a hereditary foul disease for generations;

his descendants had suffered from the ailments of wind-disease and leprosy since their childhood for two hundred years. As soon as Bodai reached the age of capping, he fell ill, and he entrusted his matter to his father and elder brothers.

"The illness will surely not recover; I fear it will bring about future calamities. I beg you to send me to the mountains. His father and elder brother packed provisions and escorted him to the base of a cliff, where they wept and departed.
Before long, he ceased eating. Suddenly, a monk passed by and took pity on him, saying, "You should recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*;
if you can internalize even a single four-line verse, you may perhaps escape this suffering. Once Bo-da began his recitation, he did not cease for several days. It was then, during the day—
A tiger approached. Fearing greatly, Bo-da closed his eyes and recited the gāthā with utmost sincerity. The tiger then licked his wounds all over;
he felt only a coolness, as if medicinal ointment had been applied, and experienced no further pain. After a long while, he looked at his own wounds and found they were all completely healed and dry.
The next morning, when the monk arrived again, Bo-da recounted the events in detail. The monk then gathered some green grass from the side of the mountain.
[The monk] took hold of it, handed it over, and said, "This can be used to wash the sores. However, upon returning home, boil this and bathe with it.
The man then wept and bowed in gratitude. The monk patted his back and departed. When he arrived home, his parents were greatly astonished; he then related the full account from beginning to end.
After bathing, his body was bright white and entirely free of sores. From that point on, the hereditary disease ceased. He recited a verse for the rest of his life. (From the *Baolin Zhuan*).
[This] should be recorded).
Seng Weigong, Wang Mian, Dong Jinzhao (the above three cases are all recorded in the *Jiuyi*),
Kang Zhongqi.
Kang Zhongqi departed for the Eastern Sea during the eleventh year of the Yuanhe era of the Tang dynasty, yet did not return for several years.

His mother had only this one son, and after a long time she missed him deeply. A monk came to beg for alms, and the mother told him her story in detail. The monk said, "Simply recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*."

The son was ill and about to return home. His mother, being illiterate, had him copy out a sutra; she then hollowed out a pillar of the house to bury it, coating the top with lacquer and paying it reverent homage morning and evening.
One night, a thunderclap shook the earth, uprooting this pillar and carrying it away. More than a month later, the son indeed returned.
He brought a great wooden log wrapped in a silk pouch to his home, where he entered and prostrated himself before his mother. When his mother questioned him, he replied: "It was my second cousin."
He said, "At sea, my boat encountered a storm and was wrecked, and I fell into the water. Suddenly there was a clap of thunder, and I cast this wood onto the waves.
I was able to float to the shore by clinging to it; thus, my life is what it granted me. How could I not revere it? His mother cried out in alarm, saying:
"It must be a pillar of my own canon. He then broke the pillar and obtained the scripture; mother and son constantly recited it together (from the *Baoying ji*).
Wu Kejiu, Wu Kejiu.
A native of Yue, he resided in Chang’an during the fifteenth year of the Yuanhe era of the Tang dynasty. He followed the Māṇiccha teachings. His wife was Wang...

The man followed her for over a year, after which his wife suddenly died. Three years later, she appeared in a dream to her husband and said, "I have become a snake due to my wrong views and am now beneath the stupa at Huangzi Pool.
I shall die tomorrow morning; I pray that you will request a monk to go there and recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, hoping thereby to escape this suffering.
The husband did not believe her in the dream and rebuked her. Enraged, the wife spat in his face, and he woke up in a startle.
Jue’s face swelled up; the pain was unbearable. His wife again dreamed that her husband’s elder brother said, "Go to the garden and take some dragon-tongue grass (*nāgavallī*);
pound it and apply it as a poultice, and he will be cured immediately. Upon waking, the brother ran to fetch it and gave it to his younger brother, who recovered at once.

The following morning, the brothers went together to invite a monk to recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Suddenly, a large snake emerged from within the stupa, raised its head, and looked about in all directions. When the sutra recitation ended, [the snake vanished].
He died; Kejiu returned to the Buddha and constantly upheld this sutra (from the *Baoying ji*).
Qian Xingli was a native of Shan Prefecture. He was illiterate, but at the beginning of the Changqing era, he constantly upheld one scroll of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

Wherever he went, he would burn incense and pay his respects. Once, while transporting goods out of Tongzhou, he encountered more than ten bandits. As they were walking along, he set down his goods and fled;
yet the load, weighing no more than fifty or sixty catties, could not be moved when the bandits tried to lift it. Staring at one another in astonishment, they were filled with wonder.

He pursued him and questioned him while he stood there. The man replied, "There was a *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* among my belongings; I feared it was due to its supernatural power. The thief opened his bag and found the scripture there.

He returned the money—amounting to over one hundred thousand [coins]—and requested the scripture, vowing never to commit robbery again and to uphold it for the rest of his life (as recorded in the *Baoying ji*).
Seng Fa-zheng; Śrāmaṇera Dao-yin (the above two cases are both recorded in the *Jiuyi*).
He Lao, He Lao:
a native of Ezhou who was formerly a merchant. He specialized in reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. During the Changqing era of the Tang dynasty, because of a hired laborer...

Carrying his goods, he rested for the night on a mountain path. Suddenly overcome by exhaustion, he fell asleep and was beheaded by a hired laborer, who threw his head into a mountain torrent and hurried to the market to sell the goods.
Upon seeing the old man He approaching, he was struck with great terror.
He said, "By the power of my recitation of the sutras, I swear not to speak of this to anyone. Thereupon, they together became monks (from the *Baoying ji*).
Gulong Yi.
Gulong Yi was a man from Jianzhou. During the Changqing era of the Tang dynasty, he supported himself by working as a laborer in Qi County.

Whenever there was someone in the village who was ill, he would go to visit them; on one such occasion, he saw that they had transcribed the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, whereupon he groundlessly destroyed it and left.
He cut it off. Upon returning home, he immediately became mute; no physician could cure him. He was stubborn, foolish, and lacked discernment, yet he never repented.
After only five or six years, he suddenly heard a neighbor reciting this sutra. Startled, he reproached himself, saying: "In the past, I slandered the True Sutra and incurred this muteness.
If I were now to repent and apologize, and venerate it for the rest of my life, would I then be able to speak? From then on, every time...

He heard [the monk] reciting the sutras and leaned against the wall, listening with single-minded concentration for over a month. He began to suspect that he had mastered the recitation after only a few days.
One day, while walking into the temple, he encountered an elderly monk and bowed to him. The monk asked, "What is the matter? whereupon [the man] pointed to his mouth to indicate that he was mute.

The monk then used a knife to cut beneath his tongue, and he was immediately able to speak. Consequently, when he recited the sutras with the monk, it was exactly like the voice of a neighbor; after a long time, [he became proficient].
He went to visit the monk, but could no longer find him. Pointing to a mural of Subhūti on the wall, [the monk] said, "This is he.
Thereupon, he transcribed the sutra and painted an image of Subhūti, prostrating before it for the rest of his life (from the *Baoying ji*).
Zhao An of Chengdu lived during the fourth year of the Tahe era of the Tang dynasty. He regularly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāraṇī* Sūtra ten times every day.
At that time, as the Mian rebels were retreating, An encountered their military equipment along the road and repeatedly collected it to take home. He was subsequently accused by his enemies.

When the officials captured him at his gate, he wept and performed prostrations according to the ritual classics before departing. He was then seized by the prison guards and subsequently falsely confessed to the crime.
As he was being led to the Hall of the Regional Commander for sentencing, his shackles and fetters fell away of their own accord. When the commander interrogated him, An replied, "I am not a thief."

They all obtained them on the streets and alleys. Every time he recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, he suspected it was due to its power. The regional commander scolded him, not believing this.
When it came to the next instance, he suddenly saw the character "release" (fang) written beneath the name Ananda, followed by the words: "The rest shall be handled according to the law."

He did not know what this meant. Upon returning, he bathed and paid homage to the scriptures. When he opened the case to look at them, the sutras were crumpled, torn, and their rollers broken, as if they had been crushed by a strong man.
His wife said, "I suddenly heard a sound from within the case, as if there were someone striking it with an axe."
Thus, when he was subjected to interrogation and examination, there was not the slightest discrepancy [between his testimony and the facts] (from the *Baoying ji*).
He Zhen, Wang Yin, and Wang Han (the above three cases are all recorded in the *Jiuyi*),
Ning Mian.
Ning Mian was a man from Yunzhong. In his youth, he possessed great courage and was skilled in horsemanship and archery;

he was capable of grappling with fierce beasts using only his physical strength, without the need for weapons. The Governor of Beidu admired his valor and appointed him as a court general (*yājàng*). Later, leading four thousand troops, he stationed his army at Feihu City.
At that time, the Commander of Jimen was arrogant and tyrannical, abandoning the laws of the Son of Heaven; a letter of rebellion reached the imperial court. The Tang...
Emperor Wenzong issued an edict for the governor of Beidu to attack from the south. Before the edict had even arrived, the troops from Jimen raided Feihu at night;
the sounds of gongs and drums shook the earth, and the people of Feihu were thrown into a state of panic, feeling no security.
They said to Ning Mian, "The Jimen soldiers are fierce and robust; they cannot be matched. They are arriving now, and the situation is extremely urgent. We pray you empty the city and flee."
Otherwise, they will attack and take our city by morning or evening. I cannot bear to see my father, sons, and brothers all fall beneath the blades of these rebels;
once it is too late, what can be done? Even if the Son of Heaven were divinely martial, how could he ever clear away my grievances? I beg you to deliberate this thoroughly.
Although I am encouraged, I consider my own troops to be few and cannot withstand the vanguard of the Ji army. I shall listen to the words of the local people, lest I incur their offense.
The Son of Heaven wished to strengthen the walls and hold his ground, yet he feared that the people of the entire district would all be slaughtered by the hands of the rebels.
His anxiety was extreme, yet he could not resolve upon a strategy. Suddenly, a spy reported: "The rebels have been completely routed; there are discarded armor and equipment beneath the city walls;
please go and retrieve them. He hurriedly ascended the city wall to look out. At that time, the moon was bright and clear, and he saw the rebel soldiers fleeing in disarray, stumbling and falling.
Those who were brought down in defeat were beyond counting. When a large army struck from behind, Yuan Mian greatly rejoiced and opened the gates of the city, releasing his troops to pursue them.

He captured dozens of men alive and seized a great quantity of abandoned armor. Previously, Mian had been fond of the Buddhist faith and often read Buddhist scriptures, including the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
After defeating the Ji commandery forces, he captured their prisoners and interrogated them. The prisoners said: "Towards evening..."
Looking up at the city wall, he saw several giants, each over twenty feet tall, magnificent and terrifying. With eyes blazing with rage and mouths agape, they stood bare-chested and grasping swords.
When the people of Ji saw them, they were struck with horror and their hair stood on end; they immediately fled to hide—how could they have had any intention of fighting?
Yuan Mian realized that these giants were actually Vajrapāṇis and marveled at this even more. Yuan Mian later served as the Minister of the Imperial Secretariat (Yushi Zhongcheng).
Later, he served as an assistant commissioner for the Qing Sai military command (as recorded in the *Xuānshì Zhì*). Ni Qín was a native of Zizhou.
In the fifth year of the Tàihé era of the Tang dynasty, he was renowned for his military prowess and was consequently appointed to oversee Xìngjiào in Fūzhou.
Cang had long been a practitioner of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. His residence had a hall that faced the river and was exceptionally magnificent.

Cang installed a Buddha image there and recited the sūtra. On the ninth day of the sixth month, the river water rose in a great flood; yet it did not reach the base of this hall. Cang redoubled his efforts in recitation.
When the waters receded, he surveyed the surrounding area for several li; all the other houses and buildings were submerged, but this hall alone remained almost entirely untouched.
It became soaked, yet the granary was not damaged at all. Everyone paid him reverence (from the *Baoying ji*).
Gao She (cited in the *Jiuyi*) and Zhang Zheng.
Zhang Zheng was a native of Qiong Prefecture. On the fifteenth day of the seventh month in the third year of the Kaicheng era of the Tang dynasty, he died suddenly.
Initially, he saw four men come to seize him; after traveling for half a day, they reached a vast river about three feet deep. Upon closer inspection, it was entirely composed of pus and blood.
He then quietly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. The messengers’ expressions changed, and they entered the city, where they saw a Hu monk eight *zhang* tall.

[He was] over one chi tall. He scolded the messenger, saying, "Why did you not follow the warrant? You have arbitrarily seized innocent people. They were all struck with alarm and prostrated themselves.

When they were brought before the King, the monk sat facing him and said, "Zhang Zheng is a disciple of my own school; he has been wrongly brought here. The King said, "Wait while I briefly interrogate him.
The monk’s expression grew angry. The King ruled that he be released. [The monk] saw that the four messengers were all dressed in large...
The monk was wearing a cangue. He went out of the city on his own business and did not see the river he was supposed to cross.
The monk said, "I am the Venerable Master whom you revere; do you recognize me? [The man] realized it was Subhūti and knew it was due to the power of upholding the sutra.
He prostrated himself repeatedly. The monk said, "Disciple, close your eyes. With a single strike of his staff, the man involuntarily let out a cry and then revived from death.
Three days had passed. Only his chest remained warm (*from the *Baoying ji*).
Li Ju was a native of Chengdu during the Tang dynasty. On the sixteenth day of the fourth month in the ninth year of the Dazhong era, he suddenly fell ill with an epidemic fever. He became dazed...

While he was in a state of dazed confusion, he saw a man who called himself the Ghost King Who Spreads Disease. He scolded Yu, saying: "You have offended me many times, yet I have not yet taken you away.
Tomorrow, three women will come with you; prepare wine and food quickly, for they are all my wives."
Jū also responded in kind, saying, "How have you come to have three wives? I hear only scoldings and whispers; I do not see anyone.
He returned four times, and on the twenty-first day, he took his leave. Jū also bowed as he saw him off. Upon returning, he felt his body become light.
He paid homage in the Buddha hall, and as he was about to eat gruel and set out again, he was suddenly blown away by the wind; he stood rooted to the spot and could not move.

It is possible. Even when one sees a great mountain range and a boundless river and sea, with people and animals standing along the shore at a loss as to where to go, after a long while a man in a yellow robe appears and asks, "Who are you? Follow me.

In only four or five paces, one already finds the mountains and rivers to be very far away. He asks again, "What good deeds have you performed? If you have done nothing to suit yourself, you will remain upon the waters.

[He] was making pigs, sheep, and so forth. Fearing that the King might question him further, Jū said, "In Chengdu Prefecture, I once led over a hundred families to perform meritorious works for the Western Paradise at Jingzhong Temple.

One wall [of a painting] was made for Dashingengcisi Temple, and I have already transcribed over five hundred scrolls of the Tripitaka, including the completion of the celebratory rites. The messenger led him away; after about fifty *li*, he saw—

There was a great city. Having entered the gate and traveled several *li*, he saw a monk on the dais, six or seven feet tall, who said to the king, "This man has cultivated goodness with a sincere heart;
he is free from deceit or flattery. The king interrogated the man in the yellow tunic: "How did you obtain this warrant?

He summoned the person who had escorted him, who replied, "I met him at the foot of the mountain and brought him here; I did not have a warrant for his arrest. The king said, "Send him away immediately," and then he saw [him].
The meritorious deeds he had performed were clearly recorded on a stele within the hall; the stone wall was wide and the inscription was located at the rear.
The messenger led him away and entered another courtyard, where he was seated and told the circumstances regarding Ju: "Wei, the Prefect of Hanzhou, has passed away."
He wished to appoint me as a Regional Inspector (Cishi), but I did not understand his intent at all. After six or seven days, he released me to return home.

I passed through twelve locations, all of which were called "Royal Mansions" (Wangyuan) and were fully guarded by attendants. At each place, they all said, "Write out one scroll of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* for us.
Upon arriving home, a messenger came to bid me farewell; he grasped my hand and also said, "I beg you for a scroll of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Immediately, I felt a headache.
Arriving beneath a stupa, he heard someone say, "I am the Venerable Dao’an. He struck his head twice with his staff, vowing, "May your resolve for the Way remain firm and steadfast.
He then awoke and saw Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva standing by his head, smiling. From that moment on, he was suddenly awakened to the truth.
His wife and children wept around him, saying, "He has been dead for seven days; only his heart remains warm. He then transcribed the sutras as he had promised.
[This entry is from] the *Baoying ji*. Wei Shi, the Magistrate of Banan in Ba Nan, constantly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
During the Guanghua era of the Tang dynasty, he arrived at Nixi and encountered a woman.

A man wearing a crimson robe was walking along with two sons. They climbed a mountain ridge together when other travelers stopped and cried out in alarm, identifying them as a mother and her three cubs of a large red fox.
The man and his children hesitated for a moment and then took a different path away from Wei, who remained entirely unaware of this.
This was due to the power of his recitation of the sutra (from the *Shuyiji*).
Yuanchu was a native of Jiujiang during the early Tang dynasty. He sold firewood in the marketplace and was seventy years old. He regularly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.

One evening, as he was returning from Jiangnan to Jiangbei, a great storm of wind and waves arose in midstream. All those traveling with him perished, yet Yuanchu alone floated upon the water. Immediately—
He drifted to the southern bank, where a fleet of moored boats all belonged to great merchants. Seeing the light several feet high upon his back, they took him for a man of noble rank;

once he had been rescued, they vied with one another to give him clothing. When he was subsequently summoned to be given food, they conversed at length until they realized he was merely a village elder.
They then questioned him about the source of the light, and he replied, "I have recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* for fifty years."

Those who carried it on their backs were protected from all preceding and subsequent calamities and hardships, none of which they failed to escape; this was known to be the power of this sutra (as recorded in the *Baoying ji*).
A military commander of Yanzhou...

During the Qiánfú era, Cui Shàngshū served as the Military Governor of Yànzhōu. His administration was characterized by severe and strict laws. Once, a military officer failed to appear for the morning audience;
Cui was greatly incensed and ordered that the officer be executed on the spot at the headquarters. After the execution, the officer’s countenance remained unchanged, which filled everyone with awe.
That night at the third watch, he returned home; his wife and children were struck with terror, believing him to be a ghost.
The object. The military commander said, "When I was first sentenced to execution by beheading, it was exactly as if I were in a drunken sleep;
there was no pain whatsoever. At midnight, I woke up to find my body lying in the street, and from that point I returned home. My wife and children knew nothing of how this had come about.

When I entered to offer my apologies the following morning, Cui was startled and asked, 'What sorcery do you possess that could cause such a thing? The commander replied, 'I have never possessed any sorcery. Since my youth, I have studied the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā*."
The scripture was recited three times daily. Because he had been reciting scriptures yesterday, the execution was delayed. Cui asked, "Do you remember when you were executed?

He replied, "When I was first led outside the戟 gate (Ji-men), I became as if intoxicated; I do not remember the time of my execution at all. Cui asked again where the scripture he had been reading was.
He said, "It is inside a locked case at home. When it was brought there, the lock remained as it was. Upon breaking the lock, the scripture was found inside.

Having already severed both [the sword], Cui was greatly alarmed. He repented and consoled the military general, subsequently bestowing upon him a set of robes and commanding that one hundred scrolls of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* be transcribed for his offering.
Today, outside the gate of Yanshou Monastery in Yanzhou stands the former office of the military general;
there, the image of the sword used to sever the sutra remains intact to this day (as recorded in the *Baoying ji*).
Yang Fugong’s younger brother was a Tang palace eunuch surnamed Yang; his personal name has been forgotten. He was the younger brother of Fugong.

For over twenty years, he remained within the rebel ranks of Qin Zongquan, Lu Yanhong, and Liu Jurong. He did nothing but recite the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Even while staying inside the besieged city, he never once...
[Li] Fei was dismissed. Zongquan appointed his son as the Regional Commander (Jiedushi) of Xiangyang, while Yang served as the Military Inspector (Jianjunshi).

Taking advantage of the people’s state of fear and anxiety, Yang incited his subordinate general Zhao Deyan to attack and kill Zongquan’s son. He then submitted a memorial recommending Deyan for appointment.
He was appointed as a Military Commissioner (Jiedushi). Consequently, the military administration gradually stabilized, and the people returned to their former livelihoods.

Yang became even more diligent and earnest in his recitation of the scriptures. Once, while he was burning incense and engaged in recitation beneath a willow tree outside the military headquarters (yamen), a scroll of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* written in golden characters suddenly flew down from the sky.
Yang prostrated himself, received it with both hands, and stood there, struck with awe and trembling.
Is it not because his mind and heart were imbued with sincere faith that he obtained this virtuous retribution?
Thus, although he was trapped among a band of rebels for twenty years, he was ultimately able to decapitate the great thieves, establish extraordinary merit, and preserve his fortune and rank;
this was surely due to the secret protection of the Buddha (from the *Baoying ji*).
Regarding the itinerant practitioner from Cai Prefecture:

During the Tang dynasty, when Tu Songwen was serving as the governor of Huangzhou, Qin Zongquan defied the imperial mandate and rose in rebellion. He intended to carry out a great plunder across the four borders.

There was a practitioner in Cai Prefecture who recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*; the people of the commandery all held him in high esteem. Consequently, Zongquan dispatched him as a spy.
He was ordered to Huangzhou to investigate matters. Before even ten days had passed since the messenger arrived at Huangzhou, he was betrayed by someone.
Song Wen was greatly incensed and ordered that the man be assembled before the military gate for execution. Suddenly, it was reported that an envoy with a promotion had arrived.

The generals and officers submitted a petition, stating that they were currently celebrating a joyful occasion and did not wish to carry out an execution so abruptly. Consequently, Song Wen merely ordered him to be placed under house arrest for over a month.
Before the envoy had arrived, the execution was again ordered. As he was being led out from the prison cell, news was reported that the envoy had entered the border;

thus, the execution was suspended once more. When the envoy had already departed, he was led out to face the execution. At that moment, the Grand General entered the yamen and, seeing him, immediately addressed Song, saying:
"Huangzhou possesses a formidable army and cavalry, and its fortifications are formidable. Why fear that a villainous rebel might be scouting for intelligence? A spy is not inherently evil."
The Party was held in subjection by others; may the General generously grant him his life as a token of clemency.

He humbly accepted this command and, having shaved his head and donned an iron collar (*kēn*), traveled to solicit donations. When the construction of the new Kaiyuan Temple was nearly complete, one night he dreamed of the Eight Vajrapāṇis, who told him:
"Monk with the iron collar, you have performed such ascetic practices; now that the building is finished, why not release your collar?"
This was done to signal his virtuous character. Wen Jue perceived this as a great marvel and subsequently ordered his shackles to be removed, treating him with exceptional courtesy.
From then on, throughout the entire province, everyone addressed him as "Venerable Vajra" (as recorded in the *Baoying ji*).
A Sea-Going Merchant of the Tang Dynasty:
There was once a wealthy merchant who constantly recited the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and always carried a copy of the scripture with him.

Once, while trading abroad, he stayed overnight on a sea island. The other merchants, coveting his wealth, conspired together to kill him. They placed his body in a large wicker basket and [covered it] with a massive...
The stones were all submerged in the sea. At dawn, as the merchant ships set sail, they realized that the island where they had anchored the night before was actually a monastery.
The monks there heard the sound of someone reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* every evening, though it came from deep beneath the seabed.
The monk was greatly amazed by this. He therefore ordered a skilled swimmer to submerge into the water to search for him. There they saw an old man reading a scripture inside a basket;
they pulled and hauled him up. The monk asked him how he had come to be there. He replied, "I was killed and cast into the sea. I did not know I was inside this basket.
Suddenly, I found myself in a palace, where people constantly brought me food and drink; I have been peaceful, happy, and at ease."
When the assembly of monks heard this, they all praised him universally; such was the spiritual efficacy of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
He then shaved his head before the monks and entered the monastic life at Shōin-ji (as recorded in the *Hōōki*).
